Tech Report: Should You Worry About That Bump on Your Chest?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin.
  • While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society.
  • According to recent reports, there isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a newly introduced bump on your chest.

According to recent reports, there isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” says Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” claims Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any latest or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”.

Your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” notes Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

Industry observers note that “This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” indicates Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

When hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” notes Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”.

Blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” states Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

Industry observers note that this condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” says Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

It has been revealed that if you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any new, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” says Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”.

Industry News: Brave Newly introduced Visions Creativity as Rebellion

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 62 min read (12395 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~62 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PhotoVogue is proud to unveil the shortlist of 100 photographers and video makers selected for Brave New Visions: Creativity as Rebellion, our Global Open Call dedicated to the power of creativity to challenge the status quo, question established narratives, and imagine alternative futures.
  • What's Next This shortlist marks the beginning of the next chapter of Brave Upcoming Visions: Creativity as Rebellion.
  • This photograph is part of the series ‘Farīsāt – Gunpowder’s Daughters’.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PhotoVogue is proud to unveil the shortlist of 100 photographers and video makers selected for Brave New Visions: Creativity as Rebellion, our Global Open Call dedicated to the power of creativity to challenge the status quo, question established narratives, and imagine alternative futures. With 95,758 submissions from 9,160 artists across 155 regions, the response to this year's Open Call was extraordinary. But beyond the numbers, what moved us most was the imagination, urgency, and creative courage of the work we received. We live in a world saturated with images. More images are produced and consumed than ever before, yet more images do not necessarily mean more understanding, more imagination, or more freedom. What matters is not simply creating something new, but finding a way to make us see, feel, or question something we might otherwise have overlooked. Perhaps today, one of the most rebellious things an artist can do is refuse to give us another image we already know. Rebellion does not always announce itself loudly. It can be political and confrontational, but it can also be intimate, poetic, playful, uncomfortable, or deeply personal. It can take the form of tenderness, humor, beauty, or an unexpected way of looking at something familiar. What makes it rebellious is the freedom to question what we have been taught to accept and to imagine what might exist beyond it. This year's Open Call brought together an extraordinary range of ideas, emotions, and visual languages. Some works confront urgent social and political realities. Others explore identity, memory, belonging, desire, or the complexities of human experience. What connects the 100 selected artists is not a shared aesthetic or a single definition of rebellion, but a willingness to take risks, experiment, and follow their own vision. Images do more than represent the world. They influence how we understand it, whose stories we recognize, and what we believe is possible. The artists presented here remind us that creativity can do more than reflect reality. It can challenge the assumptions through which we see it and make space for futures we have not yet imagined.

What's Next This shortlist marks the beginning of the next chapter of Brave Upcoming Visions: Creativity as Rebellion. In the coming weeks, we will announce which artists from the shortlist have been selected to exhibit at the next edition of the PhotoVogue Festival, as well as the three artists who will receive the PhotoVogue Grants. We will also reveal the festival's dates and location. We invite you to return to this page and follow PhotoVogue on Instagram for these announcements. Above all, we want to thank every artist who trusted us with their work. Selecting 100 artists from such an extraordinary response was incredibly difficult. This shortlist represents only a fraction of the talent, imagination, and creative courage we encountered. The future is not something we simply inherit. It is something we have the power to imagine.

Farīsāt - Gunpowder’s Daughters.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Farīsāt – Gunpowder’s Daughters’. For centuries, tbourida, the Moroccan equestrian tradition reenacting ancient Arab military manoeuvres, was an exclusively male domain. Today, women are mounting their horses, leading their own troupes and rewriting the rules of a centuries-old practice. Known as farisat, these riders are challenging the patriarchal structures that have kept them out of the arena, claiming a place in Morocco’s cultural heritage. Following several all-female sorbas across the country, Pinzi documents a quiet but determined shift in tradition, where simply taking the reins can become an act of resistance.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Heaven Belongs to You’. What if divinity had never been somewhere above us, but always within us? Okoro reimagines heaven through the presence of contemporary African subjects, casting real individuals as living mythologies whose everyday existence carries the weight of the sacred. Drawing on the power of ancestral narratives, the series challenges the mythologies that have historically dictated who is entitled to embody purity, power and the divine. Here, divinity is neither inherited nor bestowed: it belongs to everyone, and begins with the self.

We Didn't Choose to be Born Here.

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Didn’t Choose to Be Born Here’. At its heart are two contrasting responses to Apartheid: while Makepe’s grandfather fled South Africa for Botswana in search of a safer life, his great-uncle became a prominent anti-Apartheid activist and political prisoner. Blending staged portraiture, documentary photography and re-enactments, Makepe brings these histories into the present, collaborating with relatives to reconstruct memories and embody those who came before them. Through this intergenerational portrait, he examines the choices we inherit, the weight of political responsibility and how personal circumstances shape our relationship with collective struggle.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Grosse’. Taking its title from a word historically associated with shame and stigma, the project turns an insult into a means of questioning the beauty standards imposed on contemporary bodies. Through staged self-portraits, fictional imagery and distorted mirrors, the artist explores the uneasy relationship between self-acceptance and the desire to conform. Drawing on her own experience with weight-loss medication, she confronts the contradictions of a culture that encourages us to love our bodies while relentlessly urging us to change them. A recurring hybrid figure, suspended between reality and imagination, embodies the internalised gaze through which the body becomes both an object of scrutiny and a site of control.

This photograph is part of the project ‘4ever &ver &ver’, an anthology of three video works and one photographic piece exploring how young people navigate a social reality where online and offline lives increasingly overlap. Drawing on digital behaviours, everyday conversations and staged situations, Jip Schalkx examines a generation shaped by visibility, self-performance and the constant possibility of being seen. In a world where even the most mundane moments become potential content, identity and connection are increasingly negotiated through the logic of social platforms. Part observation, part personal inquiry, the four interconnected works form a fragmented yet intimate portrait of the present, where reality and fiction are never quite separate.

We Need To Talk In Whispers: Case Study of Alfred.

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Need to Talk in Whispers: Case Study of Alfred’. The project began with an unexpected discovery: a weathered notebook found on an overnight train in India, filled with handwritten notes, newspaper clippings and fragments of correspondence documenting lives marked by death and disappearance. Following these scattered traces, Bose travelled to Ebeltoft, Denmark, to investigate the story of Alfred, a man who lived with schizophrenia during the Second World War. Moving between archival research, oral histories, documentary photography and speculation, he reconstructs an inner world through the places, objects and silences left behind. At the intersection of memory and imagination, the work asks what whispers can reveal about the experiences society would rather leave unspoken.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘Untitled’, in which Peristiani turns the domestic interior into a stage for the power dynamics that shape women's lives. A space conventionally associated with intimacy and safety becomes a setting for surveillance, control and quiet acts of rebellion. Through two recurring figures, uncomfortable poses, obstructed mirrors and carefully choreographed gestures, she explores the tension between being watched and attempting to escape the gaze. Here, even the most familiar household objects become instruments of control, while the body itself becomes a means of resistance, reclaiming space through movement and disruption.

Sources indicate that this excerpt is part of video project ‘AFK (Away From Keyboard)’. First-person shooter games such as Counter-Strike offer players the chance to embody idealised versions of militarised masculinity, where dominance and aggression are built into the game itself. Drawing on his own teenage experience of struggling with masculinity and sexuality, van Gent revisits this familiar gaming environment through a queer lens. The installation features three looping animations using original 3D game models, whose subtle gestures and unexpected movements disrupt the hypermasculine behaviour expected of their characters. By introducing moments of vulnerability and ambiguity into a world built around military prowess, AFK asks what happens when masculinity refuses to play by the rules. Watch Full Video Here.

This photograph is part of the project ‘Una Storia Italiana’. Rivas Bao revisits the story of Imane Fadil, an Italian-Moroccan model and aspiring sports journalist who became a key witness in the trial surrounding Silvio Berlusconi’s infamous ‘Bunga Bunga’ parties. After testifying about the exploitation of young women at his private residence, Fadil died in suspicious circumstances in 2019, aged just 34. Combining archival material, photographs taken inside Fadil’s Milan home and AI-generated imagery, Rivas Bao reconstructs the images that were described in court but never visually documented. Reclaiming the visual language of Berlusconian television and propaganda, the project assembles a counter-narrative from the fragments of a national memory still reluctant to confront its own Me Too moment.

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Stars That Don’t Look Back’. Drawing on intimate memories shared by three generations of women in Taiwan, Chen weaves together family photographs, historical archives and literature to explore how women's lives are shaped by the forces of history. Against the backdrop of Japanese colonial rule and the White Terror, the project examines how women were represented, remembered and often silenced, from restrictions on personal appearance to the private narratives preserved in family albums. Moving between the political and the deeply personal, Chen traces the quiet resilience passed down through generations, finding in women's shared memories a fragile but enduring sense of belonging and inner peace.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘CLICHES’. Growing up in Morocco means inheriting a wealth of stories, sayings, stereotypes and beliefs that shape how we see ourselves and the world around us. Through staged photography blending documentary references, symbolism, fashion and fiction, Nassereddine Anjar revisits these familiar narratives, transforming them into images that sit between recognition and questioning. Approaching them as a living archive of shared memory, he explores the tensions between tradition and modernity, myth and everyday life, and the contradictions of a generation negotiating its relationship with heritage.

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Too Have Wings’. Growing up between places, Hajo returns to memories of his grandmother’s house outside Khartoum, where he watched pigeons take flight and find their way home. Having witnessed both the revolution and the war in Sudan before leaving once again, he now reflects on displacement from Doha, where the project was made. Through images of family, places and everyday life, he explores whether home is somewhere we return to, or something we learn to carry and rebuild within ourselves.

Brewed Reflections: The Poetry of Ataya.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘Brewed Reflections: The Poetry of Ataya’. Introduced to Salam by his uncle during childhood, Ataya, a West African tea ritual, becomes a way to reconnect with personal roots and a wider sense of belonging. Beyond the preparation and sharing of tea, these gatherings create space for conversation, debate, laughter and simply being together. In a world increasingly shaped by digital connection and individualism, Salam sees this collective ritual as a quiet form of resistance, celebrating the value of physical presence and the bonds that emerge when people take the time to gather.

If life is a video game, the graphics are great, but the plot is confusing and the tutorial is way too long.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘If life is a video game, the graphics are great, but the plot is confusing and the tutorial is way too long'. Taking Elon Musk as both subject and symbol of our age, Cedric Zellweger examines the contradictions of hyper-consumption, technological utopianism and the fantasies of global elites. Through elaborate still lifes staged with hundreds of objects and photographed on large-format analogue film, he assembles a surreal visual commentary on contemporary politics and late-stage capitalism. Part satire, part dystopian spectacle, the project draws on everything from space exploration to meme culture to ask who gets to shape our collective future, and whether it is one we actually want.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘TRANSFER’. For twenty years, Tan lived in their parents’ apartment while keeping their queer identity invisible. Now, they revisit the space as both a home and a departure lounge, a place to which they remain tied but from which they have long felt the need to escape. Through self-portraiture, the apartment becomes an imagined airport transfer station, suspended between belonging and elsewhere. In Chinese, zhuǎnjī (转机) means both “transfer” and “chance”: a small linguistic coincidence that captures the possibility of departure, transformation and a different beginning.

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Sake of Our Resistance’. Through portraits of family, friends and collaborators in Togo and its diaspora, Delali Ayivi explores resistance as an everyday practice rooted in community, creativity and mutual care. Beginning with a familiar story of an orange shared among an entire family, the project traces a belief in collective resources and responsibility across generations. Women’s organisations, village initiatives and the work of hairdressers, designers and sculptors become expressions of a quiet persistence. Accompanied by reflections from ten Togolese voices, the series asks what resistance can look like when protest is not always possible, and how simply sustaining one another can become an act of defiance.

GENESIS, WE WERE TRYING TO BUILD A HOME.

It has been revealed that this excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘Genesis, We Were Trying to Build a Home’. Drawing on her experience of growing up in the foster system, Mikhailia Petersen explores displacement as both a physical condition and something carried within the body. Through self-portraiture, performance and ritual, she returns to her relationship with her mother, inherited wounds and the histories of land and belonging in Cape Town. Menstrual blood, flowers, fire and water become materials for mourning and renewal, as Petersen confronts the legacies of colonialism, apartheid and intergenerational trauma. Rather than seeking to erase the past, the work asks how a sense of home might be rebuilt from what remains. Watch Full Video Here.

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project Praxis Modulus, by Ayomide Tejuoso aka Plantation. Spanning photography, film, installation and performance, the work constructs a contemporary Black mythology through the visual languages of Ifá, fashion imagery and African American aesthetic philosophies. Blue recurs throughout as a symbol of death, sacredness and liminality, shaping a world populated by self-portraits and portraits of other Black figures. Drawing on the visual practices of Fred Moten and Arthur Jafa, Tejuoso develops an unsettling visual universe where beauty, ritual and decadence converge, confronting the violence of necro-capitalism through acts of image-making and resistance.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘Of Animals and Us’. Over the past four years, Irina Werning has visited agricultural fairs and livestock shows in Argentina and the UK, searching for moments when people and animals seem to mirror one another. Groomed, judged and admired, they become unlikely participants in what the photographer describes as a Darwinian theatre of look-alikes. Behind the humour lies a more uneasy reflection on our relationship with animals: some share our homes and daily lives, while others remain out of sight until they reach our plates. Through images that invite a second look, Werning explores the growing distance between humans, animals and the landscapes they once shared.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the photographic project ‘Muñecas & Muñequerxs’. In its first chapter, set in Guanajuato, Mexico, Silvana Trevale explores the tradition of cartonería, the art of transforming paper and paste into figures used in play, ritual, satire and devotion. Working alongside local artisans, she documents the knowledge passed down through generations while reinterpreting familiar customs through contemporary questions of identity, gender and race. From the ceremonial destruction of Judas figures to the reinvention of a quinceañera ritual through a trans woman, the project reveals how traditions can become spaces of both preservation and resistance, continually reshaped by those who keep them alive.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘Loose Fist’. Following a violent homophobic attack in his hometown of Kathmandu, Arhant Shrestha began photographing men as a way to confront the fear and mistrust he had developed. What started as an exercise in exposure gradually became an inquiry into masculinity, intimacy and the possibility of connection. Through portraits and staged encounters with strangers and former classmates, Shrestha revisits the codes of male friendship, aggression and tenderness that shaped his own adolescence. In proposing care as an alternative to militarised masculinity, the project traces a personal journey from isolation towards a sense of community.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of ‘5BFW — 5 Bocas Fashion Week’, a project by Natasha Ribas and Allan Weber that brings fashion into the streets of Rio de Janeiro’s favela of 5B, placing its residents at the centre of the story. Local men with no previous modelling experience become the faces of a campaign that challenges conventional ideas of beauty, style and who gets to occupy fashion imagery. Designer clothes meet gold chains, scapulars and personal belongings, set against the textures of everyday life. Conceived as an unprecedented event for the community, the project uses fashion as a tool for visibility, self-recognition and the reimagining of a place too often seen through the eyes of outsiders.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘What If We Lived Among Gods?’. Dammy Twitch brings African deities into the everyday settings of contemporary Nigeria, imagining a world where the spiritual and the mundane exist side by side. Each image places a different god or goddess within familiar surroundings, challenging the distance that modern life has created from ancestral belief systems. Part visual theology, part cultural reclamation, the series insists that African spiritual traditions have not disappeared, but continue to shape the present. Rather than looking back with nostalgia, Twitch invites viewers to recognise the divine in ordinary life and reconsider what has been inherited, forgotten and kept alive.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series 'Hypnagogia'. Drawing on the fleeting state between wakefulness and sleep, Myles Loftin uses fashion photography to build a world where imagination takes the lead. Playful styling and dreamlike imagery explore the shifting boundaries between consciousness and the unconscious, softness and masculinity, fantasy and reality. With a sense of childlike wonder, the series embraces the strange freedom of the hypnagogic state, creating space for dreaming in a world that increasingly leaves little room for it.

good girls go to heaven, bad girls go wandering.

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘good girls go to heaven, bad girls go wandering’. Developed in collaboration with poet and artist Ranu Ritamalan through fieldwork across Indonesia, Brandon Lopez’s project follows lives lived outside the expected milestones of family, marriage and belonging. Moving between photography, speculative essays, poetry and string figures, the work questions how social structures shape our sense of time, direction and purpose. Its subjects include a monkey navigating Jakarta’s formal economy and a traffic officer observed through the rhythms of a single intersection. Here, wandering becomes a form of refusal: a way to imagine what might emerge beyond the destinations society sets for us.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘Newly introduced Order’. From the perspective of a young adult raised on pacifist and diplomatic ideals, Louis Roth documents Europe’s shifting relationship with militarisation amid a new arms race. Combining NATO exercises, military parades and official events with quieter scenes of everyday life, the project observes how military and civilian worlds increasingly overlap. Beginning in the Baltic states and expanding across Europe, Roth explores the ambivalence surrounding this transformation, known in Germany as Zeitenwende. His restrained visual language resists military spectacle, using photography to question how a new political reality gradually becomes part of everyday life.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘NORA’. Photographing her sixty-year-old friend, Bettina Pittaluga explores ageing as a process of continual transformation rather than disappearance. Through playful, intimate portrait sessions, the two revisit the many faces Nora has inhabited and those still to come. Against a visual culture increasingly devoted to smoothing wrinkles, erasing grey hair and concealing the passage of time, the project embraces the body's capacity for change, desire and reinvention. Made together as they grow older, the series remains open-ended, allowing identity to shift with every encounter.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘The Garden’. Made between 2020 and 2026, Ville Varumo’s work traces the unsettled feeling of living between a former home and a new city, caught between the desire to escape and the longing to put down roots. Through quiet observations of streets, strangers, nocturnal facades, a recurring white dog and, eventually, the artist’s newborn, seemingly unrelated moments begin to form a personal visual diary. Moving between public and private spaces, the photographs find the extraordinary in the everyday, reflecting on home as something continually built, lost and reimagined.

Industry observers note that this excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘No Man’s Wedding’. Through a twisted, symbolic wonderland, Carolina Dutca and Valentin Sidorenko explore the experience of war using the archetypes and rituals of folk narratives. Their story follows a man going to war as a groom approaches his wedding, descending into an underworld where he attempts to outwit death. Shells, soil and baptismal imagery become ambiguous symbols of passage, faith and mortality. Rather than documenting conflict directly, the artists draw on the language of fairy tales to examine the existential questions that war leaves in its wake.

...The Candle Whispered Them Here.

In a recent development, this excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘...The Candle Whispered Them Here’. Through analogue and tintype photography and photographic sculpture, Delali Cofie imagines an archive for Ghanaian folklore, giving stories a physical place to endure. Five figures from Ghanaian history and mythology, including Anansi, Yaa Asantewaa and Okomfo Anokye, find refuge in everyday household objects, transformed into vessels for collective memory. Blending the intimacy of oral storytelling with the permanence of photographic objects, Cofie reflects on what happens to stories as they fade from memory, and how the rituals of sharing them might keep them alive.

In a recent development, this excerpt is part of the video project ‘Fireworks on the Swamp’. Begun in 2013 and completed in 2020, Sergei Prokofiev’s work emerged from a period of political disillusionment and growing social tension in Russia. Conceived as an attempt to make art outside the expectations of the market and institutional system, the project uses pyrotechnics in a desolate, swamp-like landscape to evoke an atmosphere of hostility and uncertainty. Developed over seven years, it reflects on the limits of artistic interpretation and the possibility of experiencing reality directly, before it settles into a coherent narrative. Watch Full Video Here.

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘The Boat’. Over two years, Stein Henningsen pushed an old traditional wooden boat through winter landscapes, rowed it across open water and drift ice, and eventually set it alight in front of a glacier. Bringing fire and ice into direct confrontation, the performance turns the boat into a striking image of our relationship with the natural world. Part of Henningsen’s ongoing exploration of elemental forces, the work confronts the paralysis that often accompanies awareness of the environmental crisis, inviting viewers to experience the fragile balance between human life and the forces of nature. Watch Full Video Here.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of Elizabeth Haust’s "All About Loneliness", an evolving collection of images connected by an interest in magic, ritual, solitude and the body. Moving between self-observation and fiction, Haust treats photography as a way to give shape to experiences that resist straightforward expression. Ordinary spaces become stages for private ceremonies, while gestures and objects take on symbolic meaning. Together, the images form an intimate emotional archive, exploring vulnerability, desire, isolation and the invisible systems of belief we build to make sense of being alive.

This excerpt is part of the film ‘STARE’. Created by Bijoy Shetty in collaboration with designer Bhavya Ramesh for Bhavya Ramesh Jewellery and NorBlack NorWhite, the work explores the female form beyond the limits of expectation. Moving between softness and rage, vulnerability and strength, the film embraces femininity in its extremes, drawing on the mystical as a space for release and self-acceptance. Watch Full Video Here.

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Holy Mountains’. Bringing together the mountains of Mexico’s Chiapas highlands and the Swiss Alps, Diego Moreno creates a fictional landscape where two seemingly distant cultural worlds become mirrors of one another. Through photography, collage and graphic intervention, he draws on ancestral myths, folk tales and religious traditions to explore the ways identity is shaped by territory, colonisation and cultural mixing. The result is a personal mythology in which folklore becomes a way to revisit inherited histories and imagine new ones.

This photograph is part of the ongoing project ‘Everything I Want to Tell You’. Through a weekly exchange of images, videos and shared fantasies, Sadie Cook and Jo Pawlowska trace the ways class, illness, migration, gender and sexuality leave their marks on the body and everyday life. Moving between personal archives and staged scenes, their collaboration builds an ever-expanding visual world where memory and desire blur. Presented through large-scale installations of thousands of images, the work captures identity as something continually unsettled, taken apart and reassembled.

A bit more yellow, a bit more sour...

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘A bit more yellow, a bit more sour...’. Through portraits of friends and family, Eszter Sárkány explores the complicated relationship younger generations have with Hungarian traditions, caught between the desire to reconnect with their cultural roots and the need to distance themselves from their political appropriation. Rather than turning away from the past, she looks for ways to reinterpret it, finding in familiar rituals and symbols room for personal expression, autonomy and new forms of belonging. As Hungary enters a period of political transition, the series shifts from anger towards a more open-ended reflection on what might come next.

Please pierce your bones into mine.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the prokect "Please pierce your bones into mine", dedicated to the artist’s great-aunt, Jacoba Manders. Despite a 71-year age difference, the two shared a bond that felt more like friendship than family, becoming a way for the artist to reflect on ageing, intimacy and the experience of saying goodbye. Through images that hold both Jacoba’s history and the artist’s imagined future, the work considers what passes between generations beyond material inheritance. What remains is an emotional legacy of tenderness, resilience and truth, quietly shaping the lives of those who carry it forward.

This excerpt is part of the video installation ‘Afterparty’. In a vast desert landscape, fifty figures repeat familiar routines: gambling, scrolling, digging holes, burning books, practising yoga. Gabriel Barcia-Colombo imagines a world after collapse in which the spectacle may be over, but everyday life carries on as if nothing has happened. Structured around three pillars of contemporary life, knowledge, connection and leisure, the triptych examines our growing dependence on technology and the systems that shape what we know and believe. In its final moments, the figures turn towards the viewer, extending an invitation to join the party, or recognise we never really left. Watch Full Video Here.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘Touch’. Drawing on Alexis Kleshik’s own experience of sex work and queer life, the series explores the relationships that take shape between friends, lovers, clients, coworkers and chosen family. Working collaboratively with those they photograph, Kleshik moves between spontaneous encounters and staged scenes, using humour, styling and performance to create images grounded in agency and shared imagination. Beyond conventional definitions of intimacy, ‘Touch’ celebrates the forms of tenderness, play and belonging that emerge when people are free to define their own connections.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the project ‘The Journey Home’. Working with young people connected to four local NGOs in South Africa, Laura Pannack explores the daily journey to and from school as a space of friendship, independence and self-discovery. Through workshops, cameras change hands and participants become active image-makers, documenting their own experiences alongside the photographer. Combining analogue photography, drawings, collage and cyanotypes, the project builds a collective portrait of a generation navigating volatile environments, told through the humour, spontaneity and shifting perspectives of those who live it.

Sources indicate that this excerpt is part of the video project ‘KAPULUAN’. Rooted in the ancestral knowledge and ecological traditions of the Philippine archipelago, Gab Mejia brings together the voices of 700 Indigenous and frontline community members across 18 regions. Co-created with Indigenous women, queer youth leaders and local artists, the four-part film series weaves oral histories, poetry and traditional dance into a collective vision of Filipino identity. Against the backdrop of climate collapse and cultural displacement, ‘KAPULUAN’ becomes an act of remembrance and resistance, looking to ancestral wisdom for new ways of imagining the future. Watch Full Video Here.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Nebulous’. Born in New York to a family from Istanbul, Devin Oktar Yalkin has long experienced belonging as something split between places, shaped by migration, memory and distance. Bringing together black-and-white photographs made across different years and locations, the series traces the emotional imprint of a home that can no longer be returned to as it once was. Water, recurring throughout the images, becomes a passage between departure and return, familiarity and estrangement. Rather than documenting a place, Yalkin follows the traces it leaves behind, wherever he goes.

This photograph is part of the series "Ghosts Follow Us", exploring the spirits and changing landscapes of Isaan, northeastern Thailand. Through analogue photography, the artist documents a culture in which ghosts inhabit banyan trees, rice fields and everyday rituals, shaping the relationship between people and the natural world. Yet another kind of haunting runs through the images: an uncertain future, as shifting weather patterns unsettle generations of agricultural knowledge. Focusing particularly on the children who will inherit this changing landscape, the series captures a place suspended between ancestral beliefs, ecological loss and the passage of time.

The Architecture of Guāi (乖與不乖之間).

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘The Architecture of Guāi (乖與不乖之間)'. Returning to his former primary school in Taiwan, Adam Lin revisits the culture of discipline and obedience that shaped his childhood. At the centre is guāi, a Mandarin word used to praise children for being well-behaved and compliant. Through workshops with current students, Lin turns the classroom into a space for playful disruption, where everyday objects, gestures and postures become tools to challenge institutional rules. What emerges is a collaborative portrait of the tension between conformity and the freedom to imagine otherwise.

POR FAVOR, NO TE VAYAS / PLEASE, DONT LEAVE.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘Por Favor, No Te Vayas / Please, Don’t Leave’. After years in New York, Andrés Rios returned to Bogotá to photograph the city he grew up in and the people who make it home. Through portraits of friends, familiar streets and everyday encounters, he captures a place marked by uncertainty and contradiction, yet sustained by creativity, warmth and a sense of community. At its heart is a tension between the impulse to leave and the desire to stay, finding hope in the small, collective acts of building a life together.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Down There’. Across Mississippi, Sophia Cutino documents the networks of lesbian communities creating spaces for love, care and self-determination amid a climate of religious conservatism and anti-LGBTQ+ legislation. Through intimate 35mm portraits and handwritten notes, the project moves between private homes and shared spaces, allowing women to shape how their lives are seen and remembered. Rather than centring hardship, Cutino focuses on the everyday acts of connection, creativity and belonging through which these communities make a life on their own terms.

This photograph is part of the series ‘New Paris’. Begun when he was just seventeen, Adali Schell’s project grew out of a period of family upheaval and grief, following his move from Southern California to his mother’s hometown in rural Ohio. Turning his camera towards friends, relatives and neighbours, he builds an intimate portrait of a community through its living rooms, bedrooms and backyards. What begins as a personal record gradually opens onto a wider picture of contemporary America, where economic hardship, loss and social neglect are woven into the fabric of everyday life.

This photograph is part of the series ‘One Day I am gonna be a man’. Jonas Glanz examines looksmaxxing, an online culture of male self-optimization in which attractiveness is measured, ranked and endlessly corrected. Drawing on its visual language, from rating scales and before-and-after images to grooming routines and idealized masculine figures, he stages the male body as both an object of desire and a project under constant construction. Moving between fashion photography, still life and video, the work exposes the contradictions of a pursuit in which self-improvement becomes discipline, performance and an ideal that can never quite be reached. The photograph, 'False Adam' demonstrates a young man among apple trees, crowned with golden laurel, an artificial snake wound around his arm. In looksmaxxing, "True Adam" names the highest rank of male beauty, an ideal no one reaches. The biblical Adam is the first to feel shame about his body.

This photograph is part of the series ‘I Hope Your Family Is Safe’. After nine years abroad, Anya Tsaruk returned to Ukraine to document the lives of her loved ones during the war. Rather than focusing on destruction, she turns her attention to the quiet moments of everyday life: gestures of care, familiar places and the closeness of family and friends. With tenderness and restraint, the series reveals how ordinary experiences take on new meaning under the constant threat of war, offering a portrait of Ukraine grounded in human connection rather than distant spectacle.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Rotting from Within’. Beginning at seventeen, when he reconnected with his estranged father, Abdulhamid Kircher turned to photography to make sense of his family history and his own Turkish heritage. Combining portraits, candid observations, archival material and personal writings, he traces the generational trauma passed down through the men in his family, confronting the myths of masculinity, violence and inherited identity. Part autobiography, part visual investigation, the work explores how photography can help us approach the people closest to us, even when their histories remain partly unknowable.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Mannequins’. Using taxidermy as an unexpected departure point, the artist examines sculptural form within narrative imagery to reflect on aging, inherited femininity, and the labor behind entertainment. Moving between taxidermied figures and intimate portraits of herself and her mother, the work draws a piercing parallel between preserved animal specimens and the expectations placed on young women in Hollywood: rendered pristine, suspended in time, and meticulously packaged for consumption. Part conceptual study, part personal inquiry, the series interrogates the artifice of beauty and the cost of eternal preservation.

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Moon in Your Throat’. Asking what happens to the grief swallowed in pursuit of success, the work depicts Koreans living across the United States seated inside darkened homes, illuminated only by the faint glow of refrigerators, screens, and digital clocks. Through long-exposure portraits, contemplative still lifes, and family-photo collages, the artist explores how displacement, collective history, and unresolved emotion physically inhabit the body. Guided by the Korean concept of Han and Jung’s archetype of the shadow, the series creates a quiet space for collective mourning, asking what transformative healing might emerge when buried sorrows are finally permitted to surface.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Room 房间’. Drawn from the artist’s life lived between Chengdu and Fresh York, the work gathers tender glimpses of friends, lovers, and intimate, familiar interiors. Originally published as their debut photobook in 2025, the series functions as an architecture constructed entirely through imagery and deliberate pairings, tracing how the concept of home gradually evolved from a fixed physical location into a portable emotional state. Part visual diary, part spatial meditation, the photographs reflect on transience, connection, and the quiet spaces we assemble within ourselves to belong.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘Effigy of Man’. A decade after his passing, the artist’s grandfather endures in family photographs as a revered, often feared patriarch—a strict, orthodox figure whose temperament was indelibly forged by his displacement from Multan to Haryana during the 1947 Partition of British India. Through studio portraiture and physical collage, the artist directly intervenes in these inherited portraits to challenge dominant codes of masculinity embedded in family archives. Part reckoning, part tender excavation, the work unpicks the myth of the unyielding patriarch, suggesting that one must dismantle the monument of a man in order to truly see him.

MY HEAD IS A DESERT FULL OF TULIPS.

This photograph is part of the series ‘MY HEAD IS A DESERT FULL OF TULIPS’. Conceived as an ongoing photographic universe suspended between reality and fiction, the work captures subjects suspended in media res, leaving their relationships, histories, and interior motives deliberately unresolved. Through recurring gestures, shared hairstyles, synchronized clothing, and uncanny everyday scenarios, disparate people and landscapes begin to rhyme and echo across frames, building a fractured, collective realm. Part cinematic daydream, part surrealist taxonomy, the series distills the tension between isolation and kinship, showing how easily the familiar can tilt into the strange, the intimate, and the absurd.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘Ohnmacht’. Exploring the visceral experience of losing control over one’s body—a state of profound helplessness—the work captures women collapsing inward, where the tactile softness of their clothing clashes against stark, unforgiving environments to lay bare the weight of feminine expectations. Drawing from archival imagery of Victorian fainting spells and histories of mass hysteria, the artist uses shifting warm and cold light to expose the contradictory faces of disempowerment: fragile beauty, desperate cries for help, and latent resistance. Part psychological study, part quiet protest against patriarchal structures, the series gives tangible, enduring form to a silent exhaustion known intimately by women across generations.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Puerpera’. Born from the artist’s own birth trauma and the amnesia that enveloped the hours immediately following labor, the work offers a visceral exploration of a profound, near-universal threshold in womanhood: the disorienting stillness that arrives right after giving birth. Through intimate imagery, recorded conversations, and contemplative reflection, the series attempts to reconstruct an emotional landscape so intense, fleeting, and overwhelming that memory itself often fractures. Part personal catharsis, part raw maternal record, the project gives voice to the unspoken shock and tender vulnerability of early postpartum, reclaiming a physical reality too often eclipsed by silence.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘Neti È Kon’. Translating into "The Night is Coming," the work documents nocturnal portraits and nocturnal scenes across Suriname, capturing the enigmatic spirit of the evening through the cultural cadence of its local dialect. Imbued with a quiet intimacy where darkness evokes memory and longing, the photographs examine the subtle sensory elements that trigger a sense of belonging, redefining home not as a fixed geographical border, but as an emotional construct carried within. Part cultural ode, part lyrical meditation on displacement and longing, the series reveals how the twilight hours can bridge distance and resurrect familiar worlds.

Industry observers note that this video is part of the series ‘Hands, trees, heads, scars’. Conceived as a tender meditation on care, active listening, and hope, the work examines the fragile geography of skin and scars among amputated Ukrainian soldiers undergoing rehabilitative massage therapy in Lviv. Continuing their long-term research into relational dynamics within healthcare, Alberto Gottardo and Francesca Sironi quietly observe the gestures of solace exchanged between international practitioners and recovering servicemen like Sergei and his peers. Part clinical witness, part intimate humanitarian tribute, the series captures the quiet dignity of recovery, demonstrating how touch can transform sites of violent trauma into spaces of profound resilience and connection. Watch Full Video Here.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘Reconfigurations’. Conceived as an unbound portfolio of black-and-white figure studies, the work deliberately unsettles classical conventions of nude photography. Employing a split-field diopter, the camera folds the human form back onto itself, dissolving the boundaries between nearness and distance, the sensuous and the grotesque. Across eighteen loose, unsequenced prints, the project invites the viewer to touch, reorder, and physically recompose the imagery, transforming passive spectatorship into tactile engagement and leaving both the anatomical body and the act of looking open to endless reconfiguration.

This photograph is part of the series ‘D,D&D’. Framing the examination of one’s own life as an intentional act of role-play, the project stages an alliterative rite of passage where subconscious dreams and primal drives are confronted to forge inner strength. Moving through the shadow worlds of darkrooms and the grit of dirt, the artist harnesses photography to declare vulnerability while demanding personal power—meeting internal demons, owning forbidden desires, confronting and reshaping paternal lineage, and learning to dance with fear rather than submit to it. The series chronicles years of dedicated discipline and ritual transformation, insisting that one can actively draw destiny rather than remain doomed to it.

This photograph is part of the series ‘I owe you’. Approaching physical and emotional pain not as an isolating affliction but as a shared human threshold, the project considers discomfort as an unexpected site for connection, cooperation, and mutual care. Combining still photography and moving image, the artist studies how individuals navigate enduring suffering through subtle physical gestures, repetitive daily routines, intimate healing rituals, and collective support practices. Rather than fixating on the sensational depiction of hurt, the work investigates the quiet architectures of trust and vulnerability that emerge when bodies rely on one another through dependence, tenderness, and shared endurance.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘Joyless Sex’. Chronicling the quiet desolation of intimacy unmoored from desire, the work lays bare the unvarnished realities of clandestine side hustles, the claustrophobia of lingering in rooms with lovers already outgrown, and the fragile currency of relationships alternately discarded and desperately preserved. Photographed across Paris and Latest York from 2018 to the present day, the series captures the raw friction between loneliness and physical proximity in modern metropolises. Part unflinching diary, part contemporary social record, the images excavate the silent compromises, hidden transactions, and enduring vulnerabilities that shape life behind closed apartment doors.

Crossing the River by Feeling the Stones.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘Crossing the River by Feeling the Stones’. Rooted in a concealed bodily experience from childhood, the project charts an intimate investigation into personal desire, latent fantasy, and emerging sexuality. Moving through a tender, playful, and deliberately clumsy visual navigation, the artist traces the fluid transformations of desire as it encounters migration, displacement, and restless curiosity. The project completely reimagines the female form, liberating the body from the confines of conventional gazes and reclaiming it as a sovereign territory of exploration and self-possession.

That Moment When You Can See The Crack In The World.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘That Moment When You Can See the Crack in the World’. Using the human body as mutable raw material, the work navigates the terrain of metamorphosis, queerness, and the porous boundary separating conventional beauty from monstrosity. Within this altered universe, reality becomes elastic and physical forms are liberated from prescriptive aesthetics, recasting the deemed "abnormal" not as an aberration, but as a fertile site for radical reimagining. The series celebrates physical disruption as a portal, exposing the fissures in our rigid societal architecture to glimpse alternative ways of being.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘Near’. Bringing people, bodies, and everyday objects into unexpected physical configurations, the work allows familiar forms to dismantle their everyday functions and take on radical newly introduced possibilities. By deliberately loosening the rigid grip of established social identities, inherited norms, and conventional values, the artist constructs an open, liminal space of encounter. The series invites the individual to step beyond prescribed ways of being, creating a rare clearing where one might encounter the self—and the other—entirely anew.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘Self-Portraits of No One’. Begun in 2013 prior to the artist’s gender transition, this ongoing photographic archive utilizes their own body as both subject and canvas across domestic interiors, untamed landscapes, and staged performances to interrogate identity, visibility, and physical metamorphosis. Resisting the tidy impulse of a linear transition narrative, the work approaches self-portraiture as a radical assertion of agency—reclaiming complete visual authorship over how the evolving body is documented, perceived, and remembered. The series reflects on the fluidity of becoming, demonstrating that the self is an open, ever-shifting horizon rather than a fixed destination.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘Dublin Girls’. Exploring contemporary Irish girlhood through portraits captured across the artist’s hometown, the project is intimately rooted in her lived experience as an older sister and young Irish woman navigating sisterhood, identity, and the tender, quieter thresholds of coming of age. Moving beyond reductive cultural stereotypes and performative notions of femininity, the work captures its subjects in unvarnished authenticity, preserving an essential archive of what it feels like to discover and inhabit oneself in modern Dublin. The series celebrates the quiet resilience, vulnerability, and kinship forged on familiar streets.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Muted Ember’. The project observes younger generations navigating life in contemporary China as economic uncertainty fractures the long-held promise of steady upward mobility. Through quiet portraits and observational scenes, the work captures the quiet anxieties, disillusionment, and resilience of youth confronting a rapidly shifting social reality. Part generational portrait, part contemporary document, the series examines the tension between inherited aspirations and an uncertain future.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Sacrilegio’. Using constructed photography, the project reinterprets standard biblical imagery through the lens of modern Mexico and its northern border. By blending sacred iconography with popular culture, the work explores how religious symbols mutate when confronted with realities of violence, gender, and territorial power. Rather than challenging faith, it captures the living, breathing contradictions of contemporary devotion.

Anna Göldi: Memoria di una Strega, Rituale di Restituzione.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Anna Göldi: Memoria di una Strega, Rituale di Restituzione’. The project stems from the historical tragedy of Anna Göldi, navigating the distance between archival records and the enduring resonance of her myth. Moving between reality and imagination, the imagery opens a symbolic space of restitution where her presence and memory can be reclaimed and told anew.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘Fade into you.’. Combining original photography with subtitle stills drawn from popular media, the work uses cropping, sequencing, and visual treatment to detach familiar imagery from its initial context. Reconstructed into an altered narrative, the series examines how meaning degrades, shifts, and transforms as it circulates through systems of cultural reproduction.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Set in Stone’. The work captures the tender, fleeting connections found in daily life, grounding delicate emotions into permanence by printing the imagery directly onto stone. By anchoring transient intimacy to an unyielding surface, the series suggests that even the softest feelings leave enduring traces, holding a weight and memory that outlast time itself.

It has been revealed that this video is part of the series ‘tranSformarse’. Moving from the safe enclosure of early beginnings to the inevitable compulsion to shed one’s skin, the work serves as an ode to blooming out of step, in one's own authentic hues. By leaving behind inherited expectations to embrace the painful, miraculous nature of metamorphosis, the series stands as a vital reminder that to truly inhabit the world is, at its bravest, a lifelong act of self-transformation. Watch Full Video Here.

EL TIGRE ME PERSIGUE (The Tiger Pursues Me).

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘EL TIGRE ME PERSIGUE (The Tiger Pursues Me)’. Created by Alcira Angelo, the project is an intimate photographic odyssey that explores self-discovery through the emotional and psychological terrain of duelo—a concept evoking both inner struggle and the reckoning that follows loss. The work unfolds as a visual dialogue with the self and others, constructing a quiet yet insistent collective portrait of grief and resilience.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘My friend, Whisky’. The project chronicles the eight-year creative bond between photographer Fee-Gloria Grönemeyer and her muse and collaborator, Whisky Boonjongrux. Having developed multiple photographic dialogues together that consistently push both toward latest creative horizons, the series stands as an intimate reflection on artistic trust, mutual growth, and the quiet courage required to be wholly oneself.

This photograph is part of the series ‘UNCOOL’. A study in visibility, embodiment, and representation, the project brings together twenty-seven portraits of individuals with disabilities and visible physical differences. Informed by the artist’s lived experience as a wheelchair user, the work examines how bodies are perceived, categorized, and normalized through imagery, critically questioning which bodies are granted visibility, under what conditions, and through which prevailing visual conventions.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘Matriphagie’. The project investigates how societal structures transmit and internalize prescribed norms of femininity from an early age. Structured around interviews and encounters with young girls aged four to eleven, the work uses their testimonies—balancing between learned clichés and instinctive transgressions—to ground a visual inquiry into the ambivalences, tensions, and shifting definitions of the feminine.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘Look at me like you love me’. Informed by the artist’s identity as a queer, nonbinary individual, the work explores the complexities of personhood, desire, intimacy, and family. Motivated by an existential search for self-understanding and human connection, the project centers on the radical necessity of living authentically and the mutual power of seeing and being seen, using intimate storytelling to invite viewers into deep reflection on their own identities and relationships.

This photograph is part of the series ‘t-fags’. Bringing together photographs and interviews with trans men, transmasculine, and non-binary people who identify with the reclaimed term ‘fag’, the project explores masculinities that openly embrace femininity and gender expansiveness. By challenging heteronormative expectations around gender transition, the work documents a community asserting radical self-definition. Created between 2022 and 2025, the series was self-published as a limited-edition artist book in 2026, serving as a vital archive of contemporary queer identity.

This photograph is part of the series ‘People’. Built on friendship, attraction, and creative collaboration, this ongoing portrait project actively reclaims who is pictured as desirable and who holds the authority behind the lens. Centering disabled subjects through the perspective of a gay, disabled photographer, the work employs nudity, fashion, and playful experimentation to capture beauty infused with sexual confidence, humor, and unfiltered desire.

I Love My Friends But They’re Killing Me.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘I Love My Friends But They Are Killing Me’. The project examines contemporary beauty standards and their psychological toll through portraits of young Indian women navigating micro-celebrity—influencers, reality television figures, and aspiring actors pictured inside their private bedrooms and homes. Shot primarily on 35mm film with harsh direct flash and framed by episodic, reality-TV-style text, the work strikes a deliberate tension between cultural critique, intimate vulnerability, and biting absurdity.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Cut from the Street’. The project examines hair as a medium of self-expression, identity, and resistance among young men across north and central Chennai. Through portraits and interviews, the work interrogates how caste, class, skin tone, and urban geography dictate who is granted social legitimacy and visibility. Highlighting how identical aesthetics celebrated as fashion on privileged bodies are condemned as “indecent” or suspicious on others, the series reveals everyday styling as an act of defiance—a vital claim to presence and the right to be seen.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘TOPS’. Extending the world of the companion short film, the work gathers intimate moments captured before, during, and after production to trace the profound physical and emotional journey of top surgery. Through quiet, behind-the-scenes glimpses, the collection documents the urgency of gender-affirming care, the essential networks of community support that sustain it, and the deep vulnerability that shapes the path toward embodied self-realization.

The Water Bring We, The Water Wanna Take We Back.

This photograph is part of the series 'The Water Bring We, The Water Wanna Take We Back', a project that explores the Gullah Geechee corridor as a landscape of memory, survival, and spiritual continuity. Drawing on a Gullah proverb and the Bakongo cosmogram, the project examines water as both rupture and return—marking histories of the Middle Passage while sustaining cultural resilience. Through photographs of the Low Country, the work considers how Geechee communities navigate displacement, climate change, and enduring ancestral presence.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Who’s Afraid of the Bad Wolf?’. Documenting the bedroom as the foundational universe of childhood, the work explores a space where solitude, play, and resilience are first tested, and where fantasy and reality seamlessly coexist. Centered on the intimate bedtime rituals invented by children to cultivate safety and ward off fear, the ongoing archive presently traces the private domestic worlds of eleven children across Piedmont, Italy.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘An Anatomy of Fear’. Reflecting on fear as a collective condition shaped by uncertainty, instability and the accelerating pace of contemporary life, Alvaro Deprit explores the fragile territory between identity and transformation. Through images of unfinished clay and plaster sculptures, alongside the students who inhabit the art school where the work was made, he draws a parallel between bodies and forms in the process of becoming. Adolescence emerges as a particularly charged moment of this transition, when identity remains fluid and the boundaries between vulnerability and possibility are still being negotiated.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘Thoughts, Feelings, Behaviour’. Begun in 2024, the project employs staged photography to interrogate narcissistic self-image, emotional isolation, and the alienating demands of the capitalist attention economy. Exploring the fraught boundary between self-sufficiency and raw vulnerability, the work navigates currents of desire, aggression, and melancholy. Through an experimental synthesis of body paint, collage, and sculptural props, the imagery blurs the lines between lens-based practice, painting, and tactile material experience.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Ọ Hụrụ M’—translating to “She Saw Me” in the artist’s native tongue, Igbo. Conceived as an intimate dialogue across her past, present, and future selves, this self-portrait project treats the camera lens as both a transformative portal and an unbound playground. Navigating life as a young Nigerian woman raised in the United States, the artist claims absolute authorship over her representation. Standing firmly as both creator and subject, she transforms self-imaging into a sovereign act of agency, radical ownership, and resistance against cultural erasure.

Rose Sarajevo: Girls from the East.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘Rose Sarajevo: Girls from the East’. Weaving together portraits of young women, local architecture, and surrounding nature, the project traces the enduring scars of conflict across an urban landscape under quiet reconstruction—most visibly marked by the “Sarajevo Roses,” mortar damage filled with red resin to memorialize fallen lives. Guided by fragmented memories, the artist undertakes an intimate quest for the origins of her own identity, using photography as an act of personal and historical reconciliation, an attempt to mend and bridge the fractures of time.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘Home Story’. Combining documentary and staged photography, the project unearths fragmented, visceral narratives within a space fundamentally promised as a sanctuary: the domestic home. Acknowledging the difficulty of articulating trauma into daily reality, the work interrogates how patriarchal structures isolate survivors of domestic violence into silenced, individualized tragedies. By confronting the quiet complicity of institutional secrecy, the imagery functions as an act of disclosure—insisting that giving voice to these hidden experiences dismantles the systemic machinery that thrives on their suppression.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘Scarlet Spirit’. Grounded in the enduring legacy of the 1947 Partition of India, the project traces the artist’s familial migration through ancestral memory and oral histories gathered across Kolkata’s refugee colonies. Synthesizing contemporary portraits, archival material, and surreal visual metaphors, the work constructs a layered archive of displacement that interrogates severed roots, cultural erasure, and collective resilience. Created in resonance with the milestone commemorations of Partition, the series links generational trauma and the arduous labor of rebuilding to the broader, ongoing realities of global displacement today.

The Drying Leaves: A Domestic Cartography Initiative.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘The Drying Leaves : A Domestic Cartography Initiative’. Set beneath the ancestral neem tree of Suktara, the work adopts the seasonal descent of winter leaves as a poignant metaphor for the passage of time and human mortality. Through a three-dimensional visual approach that weaves together photography, family archives, and spoken histories, the initiative maps intimate domestic geographies to resist alienation and stave off the "third death"—the quiet disappearance that occurs when a person’s name is spoken for the very last time.

Everything I Am or Have Since Become.

It has been revealed that this video is part of the series ‘Everything I Am or Have Since Become’. Centering on the elemental nature of water as a metaphor for queer safety—at once life-giving sanctuary and volatile peril—the project weaves together collective oral histories, writings, and movement developed collaboratively with an all-queer cast and crew. Created by diasporic artists navigating Fresh York City in resistance to systemic precarity, the work follows three figures across aquatic terrains in ritualistic choreography. Through sustained cycles of grief, repetition, and bodily rebirth, the series meditates on the search for refuge in hostile environments, embodying the fluid, precarious nature of both sanctuary and identity. Watch Full Video Here.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the project ‘Driving License’. Exploring an online subculture where people buy and sell photographs of other people’s faces to use as their own, Lean Lui examines the shifting boundaries between identity, ownership and authenticity in the digital age. Through a three-month investigation in which she actively participated in these transactions, Lui explores how a face can become a commodity, a disguise or a new identity altogether. The work questions what it means to be seen, and whether an image can stand in for a person who does not exist.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘Mixed / Unmistakably You’. Created by Norwegian-Indian artist Dev Dhunsi, the project takes the artist’s own mixed heritage as an inquiry into the nuances of cultural and personal identity. In a society where language lacks a direct term for mixedness, the work pairs photography and text to articulate experiences that have long remained unnamed. Interrogating how belonging, visibility, and intimacy are mediated by race, gender, and desire, the series constructs a luminous visual vocabulary for self-definition beyond existing cultural lexicons.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Constructed Portrait’. In an era marked by frictionless image oversaturation, the project investigates the blurred boundaries between the tangible and the synthetic. Confronting the extractive reality of digital photography—where personal images are systematically harvested as training data for artificial intelligence—the artist restricts the source material strictly to their own intimate photo archive. By algorithmically synthesizing and deconstructing these personal traces into a self-portrait, the work deploys technology against itself, functioning simultaneously as an ethical data citation, a formal technical critique, and an enduring act of self-reflection.

This video is part of the series ‘Nox’. Drawing from Rio Nakada’s lived experiences of complex PTSD, dissociation, and Alice in Wonderland Syndrome, the work translates internal psychological instability into an embodied sensory environment. Through fractured memories, shifting architectures, mirrored reflections, and visceral bodily distortions, the imagery renders an otherwise invisible, disorienting mental landscape spatial and tangible. Selected for the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, the project functions as an intimate bridge between isolation and communion, inviting the viewer into a briefly shared architecture of altered perception. Watch Full Video Here.

We Knew the World in Fragments of Color.

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Knew the World in Fragments of Color’. Reflecting on the personal journey of migration from Venezuela to the United States, the project explores the dislocating experience of diaspora, cultural belonging, and the fractured nature of memory. Through meticulous staged compositions and handcrafted wearable constructions, the work harnesses heightened chromatic symbolism to reconstruct a displaced home, transforming personal nostalgia into a vivid, allegorical visual language.

Meet the international jury of Brave Newly introduced Visions: Creativity as Rebellion, bringing together artists, photographers, editors, curators, and creative voices from different disciplines and backgrounds. Together with the Vogue and Condé Nast Committee, comprising more than 100 editorial and creative professionals from across our global brands, these jurors have brought their individual perspectives and sensibilities to the selection process. Their participation reflects something fundamental to PhotoVogue's philosophy: there is no single authority on what makes an image meaningful, no universal definition of beauty, and no one way of seeing the world. It is through the encounter of different perspectives that new possibilities emerge.

Photographer, Filmmaker & Curator.

Born in Addis Ababa in 1974, Aïda graduated from Howard University with a degree in Communications, majoring in Film. Her photography is in major collections including MoMA, the Smithsonian, and the RISD Museum. She’s received numerous awards, including the EU Prize in Bamako, the CRAF Award, and the Royal Photographic Society Award. Aïda co-curated the Nobel Peace Prize exhibition in 2019 and was a commissioned artist in 2020. A Canon ambassador and founder of Addis Foto Fest and Africa Foto Fair, she also leads Africa Print House and advocates for health, the environment, and photography across Africa.

According to recent reports, alex Consani is a model and actress who was named 2024 Model of the Year at the Fashion Awards in London, becoming the first transgender woman to receive the award. A face of Gucci and YSL Beauty, she has graced the digital cover of American Vogue and made history as one of the first transgender women to walk the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. Her acting credits include American Horror Story: 13 and A24’s upcoming film Peaked.

Curator, Founder & Artistic Director, Culture Art Society (CAS).

Sources indicate that awa Konaté is an independent curator, cultural strategist, and founder of Culture Art Society (CAS), a platform dedicated to research, exhibitions, and critical discourse on African and diasporic visual arts. Her practice draws on archival research, Black feminist pedagogies, and memory work, with a focus on interdisciplinary and lens-based practices by artists of African descent. She has collaborated with institutions including Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, Serpentine Galleries, Raven Row, and the Barbican, and served on juries for Rencontres de Bamako and BlackStar Film Festival. Her writing has appeared in Third Text, Foam Magazine, and Phaidon, among other publications.

Director, Foto Colectania (Barcelona).

Elisa Medde is an Art Historian specializing in Photography and Visual Culture, focusing on image, communication, and power structures. She has chaired juries for awards like the Luma Rencontres Book Award and MAST Foundation Grant. Elisa collaborates with European universities including ECAL, HSLU, and UWE Bristol. She has curated photobooks and exhibitions, with writings in FlashArt, Time Magazine, Vogue Italia, and more. Editor-in-Chief of Foam Magazine (2012–2023), she won two Lucie Awards and received the 2023 Royal Photographic Society Award for outstanding achievement in Photography Publishing.

Global Head of Photography, The Guardian.

Fiona has over 20 years of picture editing experience across newspapers and is a curator, speaker on photojournalism, and mentor in the photography community. She was picture editor of The Guardian for ten years before becoming Head of Photography for Guardian News and Media Group. Fiona covered major historic events like 9/11, global conflicts, natural disasters, and refugee crises. She has judged awards including the Sony World Photography Awards, Taylor Wessing Portrait Prize, and chaired the 2024 World Press Photo Awards jury. Fiona also serves on the board of Stills Gallery, Edinburgh.

According to recent reports, florence Bourgeois has been Director of Paris Photo since 2015. With a background spanning fashion, luxury, and the art world, she previously held positions at Givenchy Parfums, Artcurial, and the Pavillon des Arts et du Design (PAD) in Paris and London. At Paris Photo, she has introduced initiatives including PRISMES, Emergence, and Elles x Paris Photo, developed in partnership with the French Ministry of Culture and Kering’s Women In Motion to increase the visibility and recognition of women artists.
