  • In a recent development, he’ll be ready for the wilderness at a moment’s notice, even if the wilderness hasn’t called yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there’s a guy on every gift list who dresses like he lives off the land, even though the land he lives off is mostly takeout. He’s got the waxed jacket, the wool socks, and a thermos he treats like a family heirloom. He’s never had to use any of it in an emergency, but if the moment ever comes, he’ll be the best-dressed guy in the woods.

Industry observers note that lucky for you, Huckberry was made exactly for this guy. I went on a full expedition for gifts that are tough enough for the real thing and good-looking enough to wear every day: a ballistic nylon Filson briefcase, Japanese selvedge denim, elk leather Hestra gloves, and even a Jeff Goldblum perfume that smells like a campfire in the best way. It’s gear with real craftsmanship behind it, the kind he’ll reach for constantly. Will he ever actually need any of it? Unclear. Will he look great not needing it? Absolutely.

In a recent development, he’ll be ready for the wilderness at a moment’s notice, even if the wilderness hasn’t called yet. Until it does, pick any of these and you’re covered, no camping required.

It has been revealed that made from ballistic nylon, which is a fancy way of saying it can take a beating. The bridle leather handles keep it handsome enough for a meeting, all while being tough enough to survive getting tossed in the back of a truck he doesn’t own.

The official footwear of the guy whose favorite trail runs from the couch to the fridge. Cozy enough to lounge in all weekend and good-looking enough that he’ll “accidentally” wear them to get the mail.

Recent findings suggest that for the guy who insists vinyl just sounds warmer, despite not having the tech to prove it. The built-in preamp means it plugs straight into speakers, so there’s no excuse not to finally play that record he bought for the cover.

In a recent development, yes, it's a Jeff Goldblum fragrance, and yes, it's actually great. Brain Dead's collab opens with sandalwood, tobacco leaf, and leather, so it smells like a campfire at a very nice lodge. He'll get compliments, and he'll credit Jeff.

According to recent reports, every guy deserves a proper cup for a post-hike pour, and this earthy little vessel from Danny D's Mud Shop has way more charm than a plastic shot glass. Use it for whiskey, espresso, or whatever he's toasting with.

Japanese selvedge with all the rugged good looks and none of the miserable, stiff-as-cardboard break-in period. Ideal for a man of action, or at least a man who looks great standing next to a campfire.

Sources indicate that the kind of sweater that looks like it was passed down from a grandfather who really knew how to chop wood. The two-tone brown and black knit goes with everything from denim to cords, and it'll only get better with every passing winter.

Industry observers note that barbour has been dressing guys for the countryside for over a century, and this quilted jacket is the easiest way in. It's light enough to layer under a heavier coat or wear solo on crisp days, and the sage green is outdoorsy without being too literal.

Hamilton made watches for soldiers in the field, so this one is technically military-grade, even if his toughest mission is brunch. It’s hand-wound, which means he gets a small, satisfying daily ritual and a great excuse to say “my mechanical watch” out loud.

Hestra has been making gloves in Sweden since the 1930s, so it knows a thing or two about cold. These pair soft elk leather with a fleece lining: warm enough for a snowy hike, sleek enough that he won't look headed for the slopes.

Industry observers note that rototo is a Japanese knitwear brand, and this scarf has the kind of craftsmanship you can feel. The lightweight wool-cotton blend keeps him warm without the itch or the bulk, so he can wear it from first frost straight through to spring. It also has a little artisanal cred, which he’ll absolutely bring up when someone compliments it.

In a recent development, RRL is Ralph Lauren’s love letter to rugged Americana, and this plaid workshirt is the most convincing ranch hand costume money can buy. It’s built like the real thing and looks broken in on day one, ready for chopping wood or, more realistically, a Saturday at the bar.

#226660. The Best Japanese Restaurants in London, From Omakase Counters to Neighborhood Gems

The Best Japanese Restaurants in London, From Omakase Counters to Neighborhood Gems

📅 29 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding good Japanese food in London hasn’t always been the easiest task, given the city’s abundance of mediocre sushi takeaway spots and gaudy central London restaurants serving sub-par fish dressed up with too many bells and whistles.
  • Sources indicate that but in truth, you don’t need to break the bank to eat Japanese food well in London: just take the well-priced lunch set menu at Kiku Mayfair, or the reliably fresh sushi at any Eat Tokyo outpost, or the excellent quality-to-price ratio at Bond Street institution Chisou.
  • From exclusive six-seat counters to beloved West End izakayas, here is our definitive guide to the Japanese restaurants in London that are truly worth the hype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding good Japanese food in London hasn’t always been the easiest task, given the city’s abundance of mediocre sushi takeaway spots and gaudy central London restaurants serving sub-par fish dressed up with too many bells and whistles. (No piece of sushi has ever needed gold leaf so liberally applied.) Historically, to eat well, you’ve had to splurge: it isn’t cheap, after all, to source top-quality fish in the British capital, and it’s still worth saving your pennies for a blowout meal at one of the city’s top omakase counters, such as Sushi Kanesaka or Sushi Tetsu.

Sources indicate that but in truth, you don’t need to break the bank to eat Japanese food well in London: just take the well-priced lunch set menu at Kiku Mayfair, or the reliably fresh sushi at any Eat Tokyo outpost, or the excellent quality-to-price ratio at Bond Street institution Chisou. (Its former location next to the old Condé Nast offices on Hanover Square led it to be nicknamed the “Vogue canteen.”) And that’s without mentioning beloved neighborhood spots like Uchi Hackney or Jin Kichi in Hampstead.

From exclusive six-seat counters to beloved West End izakayas, here is our definitive guide to the Japanese restaurants in London that are truly worth the hype.

Located within the ritzy 45 Park Lane hotel, this Michelin-starred, omakase-only destination with 13 seats is as atmospheric a sushi experience as you’ll find anywhere in London. Step through the discreet noren curtain that marks the entrance, and you’ll feel as if you entered a portal straight to Kyoto, with the gently lit interiors—all hinoki wood, lime plaster walls, and intricate kumiko lattice work—serving as a delicate backdrop for the equally delicate flight of dishes that follows. Helmed by legendary chef Shinji Kanesaka, the 13-seat restaurant offers a masterclass in traditional Edomae-style omakase using an impressive array of locally sourced ingredients: a silky pot of chawanmushi topped with the briny sweetness of fresh Cornish crab; marbled, melt-in-your-mouth fatty tuna nigiri with perfectly seasoned rice sourced from Japan’s Yamagata Prefecture; a Scottish lobster presented on a board then whizzed up into shatteringly crisp morsels of tempura. With a price tag of £420 per person, it isn’t for the faint of heart—but for those seeking true perfection, it’s London’s ultimate bucket-list sushi destination. —Liam Hess.

Sources indicate that A true Mayfair stalwart, Kiku has been serving the neighborhood since 1978, making it one of the oldest Japanese restaurants in the city—and unlike some of its flashier neighboring sushi restaurants, Kiku’s vibe is one of calm, quiet elegance. It’s the place to go for a consistently excellent, no-frills sushi experience where the quality of the fish speaks for itself, whether it’s the salmon and tuna in a classic sashimi set, or rare delicacies like Hokkaido sea urchin and sweet prawn served on perfectly seasoned rice. The tempura here is world-class, with a light, lace-like batter, and the £40 lunchtime set menu—which consists of yakitori, tempura, sushi, miso soup, and a dessert—is one of the best deals in central London. The ultimate seal of approval? It’s a favorite spot among the staff at the nearby Japanese Embassy on Piccadilly. —L.H.

In a recent development, this low-key but stylish joint, which opened in 2024 in a bijou shopfront on Brewer Street, is the brainchild of chef Takamasa Mogi—also the founder of popular Mayfair spot Cubé—and serves up astonishingly good sushi to the 10 seats that surround its subdued but stylish hinoki wood counter. (Soho regulars will remember the building’s former life as a manga store and karaoke bar—it turns out there’s still a karaoke room downstairs if your omakase dinner ends up getting a little raucous.) I was especially impressed by the creative but not overdone nigiri, including smoky slivers of seared Korean turbot and Spanish tuna with Oscietra caviar, served atop pillowy beds of red vinegar-seasoned rice. Given the quality, it’s excellent value too: the lunchtime menu offers salad, seven pieces of omakase nigiri, and dessert for £51.80, while the dinner menu of two appetizers, nine pieces of omakase nigiri, a temaki roll, and dessert comes to £89. (They also do a well-priced pre-theater menu if you’re planning to catch a West End show.) —L.H.

Under former Noma sommelier Yuki Kaneko’s ownership, Yuki Bar has transcended East London’s small plates and orange wine scene. Within the low-lit, 20-cover spot soundtracked by disco J-pop, dishes riff on French and Nordic classics with Japanese inflections, like a sesame-studded take on oeufs mayonnaise, embracing home-style cooking and a choose-your-own-adventure menu of “snacks, littles, and larges.” A few portions of house-made potato crisps with sansho pepper and grilled onigiri kick the evening off, while rotating mains have included an aromatic chicken hot pot and blushing strips of beef tataki silken with soy sauce and mustard. Go with a group, be greedy, and get a few bottles recommended by Kaneko. —Anna Cafolla.

It has been revealed that mayfair isn’t exactly short on high-end sushi counters, so it takes serious pedigree to make a splashy entrance here. One of the few people capable of that is Shogo Amamoto, the Fukuoka-born chef behind Taipei’s two-Michelin-starred Sushi Amamoto—a reservation so notoriously tough to secure that die-hard sushi-heads are known to blueprint trips to Taiwan around it. (Sushi mastery clearly runs in the family: his brother, Masamichi, helms Tokyo’s cult-favorite Higashiazabu Amamoto.) Chef Shogo’s London outpost forgoes the usual Mayfair glitz in favor of a serene, minimalist room centered around a pale hinoki wood counter and bespoke Japanese ceramics, and the focus lies firmly in classic Edomae culinary craft. Dishes feature top-tier seafood flown in from Tokyo’s Toyosu Market alongside standout European catches—translucent slices of French wild seabass sashimi with shiso flower and ponzu, a sweet seared Orkney scallop wrapped in crisp nori, or rich, smoky nodoguro whose skin crackles straight off the grill—and warm, perfectly seasoned rice. It’s purist without feeling oppressively solemn—and one of the freshest (in every sense) fresh additions to London’s luxury sushi roster. —L.H.

One of London’s sexiest counter seats (and that’s saying something), Ushio arrives from Fukuoka, on Japan’s Kyushu island. Its first European location, Ushio serves A5 wagyu omakase style (no sushi here!), specifically akami wagyu that has been imported from Japan. It’s leaner and higher in protein, with a taste that will unfurl across an incisive multi-course menu of wagyu every which way. You’ll get a card that tells you which prime cut of beef you’re eating with every course, and it’s certainly a journey. Some are barely kissed by the grill, others draped in a rich sukiyaki marinade or glazed in their signature tare sauce. A trio of tenderloin, tongue, and kurimi are delicately salted and presented gloriously as is. (My tip? Say yes to the extra curry course! If it wasn’t so sophisticated in there, I would be licking the bowl. Add the sake pairing and enjoy your time with the very charming sommelier too.) Finish with a (meatless, but still mighty) matcha choux puff. In a quiet, darkened corridor of Fitzrovia, the minimal interiors are stunning and sleek, just like the Fukuoka flagship, built around wood and stone with Ko-Imari porcelains and hand-built ceramics by Taeko Kajihara. And everyone who works there just seems cool! A spot that lingers long on the palate. —A.C.

Tucked behind a bright white storefront in Clerkenwell, this seven-person omakase experience is among the city’s toughest reservations to secure. Husband-and-wife duo Harumi and Toru Takahashi are behind the operation (the latter being the chef), both of whom are famously warm and welcoming, fostering a convivial atmosphere versus the buttoned-up formality of traditional omakase settings. The seasonal menu relies on what is strongest in the market that day, but expect sushi so fresh it melts in your mouth and impeccable sake pairings. The restaurant sits along Jerusalem Passage, an 18th-century path to the priory of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, which later transformed into a pedestrian walkway linking St John’s Square to Aylesbury Street. —Nicole Kliest.

According to recent reports, if you’re craving sushi but aren’t in the mood for a formal omakase environment, Uchi Hackney achieves an exceptional balance. This ultra-cozy spot in a residential area of Hackney leans on traditional Japanese design motifs (linen, ceramics, wood), and even encourages guests to kick off their shoes and slip into a pair of provided slippers. The restaurant began as a delivery service in 2015 and now offers a high-quality menu in its brick-and-mortar location, serving both brunch and dinner. As for the dishes, expect a variety of hot favorites such as grilled pork belly skewers and lightly deep-fried tofu, and savor the selection of fresh sushi and sake to round out the experience. (An aside: Uchi Hackney’s intimate ambience makes for the perfect date night locale.) —N.K.

Set on the ninth-floor Liverpool Street branch of Los Mochis, arriving at Luna Omakase comes with a delightful sense of ceremony. As the evening begins, you’ll be guided with your group from the bar along a nondescript corridor to a set of sliding doors that are opened—with plenty of theatrical flourish—to reveal the 12-seater dining room, where a sculptural timber counter is lit with a lunar glow against a backdrop of glittering skyline views of the City. Over the course of 12 seasonal plates, the vibe is lively and conversational, as the sushi masters hand each pristine slice of aged fish—think melt-in-your-mouth otoro tartare with Oscietra caviar served with a cloud of smoke, or juicy king crab leg nigiri with feathery shavings of yuzu—and artfully balance traditional technique and off-the-cuff flourishes throughout the meal. (If you fancy it, you can also make the evening more spirited—quite literally—courtesy of the tightly curated list of rare sakes and Japanese whiskies that the team is more than happy to geek out over, and that will serve as an instant conversation starter with your fellow sushi obsessives.) It’s intimate and undeniably stylish, but free of the stuffiness that can make your typical high-end omakase experience feel a little intimidating. —L.H.

In operation for nearly 30 years, this beloved sushi institution now operates across eight outposts in London (plus six in Tokyo). For those who favor great value and generous portion sizes, this restaurant chain consistently gets top marks. Choose from a menu of sushi, sashimi, nigiri, chirashi, unagi, or opt for a bento box to get the full experience. Their latest creation worth dining out for? Wagyu with black tobiko (or a ‘sushi taco’, as it’s so nicknamed). —N.K.

In a recent development, this Japanese udon noodle bar opened its doors in Soho back in 2010 and has since expanded to three popular London locations, plus a shop offering provisions such as chilli oil and jars of Fukujinzuke. The original location is worth a visit for the freshly made noodles and dashi alone, but don’t sleep on the weekly blackboard specials either (previous highlights include grilled corn with miso butter and fried whitebait with shibazuke cucumber). Koya Soho is walk-ins only and is open from breakfast through to dinner. —N.K.

It has been revealed that this is where you go when you want authentic Japanese food and a killer sake selection, all in a calm, relaxed setting. Chisou’s two central London locations—Mayfair and Knightsbridge—treat guests to seasonally changing dishes and a menu of wow-worthy raw fish, with the option to sit at a sushi bar or at an intimate table. And back to the sake for a moment: Chisou prides itself on having one of the largest menus around, with experts on hand to suggest pairings and special events like sake and British cheese pairing classes led by specialists. —N.K.

Recent findings suggest that A charming, intimate spot tucked away on New Quebec Street in Marylebone, Roketsu recently relaunched as a rare example in London of kappo-style dining, where the chefs will whip up a customized set menu based on a conversation about your preferences at the beginning of the meal. The team of chefs here take a creative approach to classic Japanese cuisine, folding in a handful of French flourishes: most notably, perhaps, with one of the restaurant’s signature dishes, an opening bite of a crisp wafer filled with 10-day miso-marinated foie gras. (Other highlights included Cornish cod with a vibrant nori sauce, and flame-grilled wagyu beef with yuzu oroshi for a clean, citrus-forward finish.) With an open kitchen behind a hinoki wood counter, Roketsu is an elevated, classically Japanese dining experience—but it also comes with an element of choose-your-own-adventure fun that makes it feel genuinely unique. —L.H.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re seeking a quirkier spin on omakase dining, head over to Notting Hill, where you’ll find the six-seat Juno hidden in a speakeasy-like space at the back of Los Mochis, the popular neighborhood Mexican-Japanese restaurant on Uxbridge St. The dining room’s delightfully funky, “Tokyo-meets-Tulum” decor—bamboo, seagrass, high-gloss wallpaper—should serve as an initial clue for what to expect here: the textures and flavors of Japanese cuisine are lent a fresh twist courtesy of a bold, Mexican-inspired toolkit of spices, acids, and smoke. (Think chutoro spiked with a sharp kick of fermented jalapeño, or red bream brushed with lime aioli and topped with a sprinkle of crushed-up Oaxacan flying ant for a surprisingly delicious note of nutty earthiness.) Bring your friends and make it a party. —L.H.

There are few more scenic spots for lunchtime sushi in London than chef Endo Kazutoshi’s rooftop restaurant, which sits proudly above the Raffles London hotel at the Old War Office—and trades the monastic restraint of Endo’s Michelin-starred White City flagship for sweeping views over Horse Guards Parade. Grab an outdoor table and browse a menu that bridges Japanese precision with Mediterranean flourishes, the latter a direct nod to the years Kazutoshi spent cooking in Spain. Most of the dishes are built for sharing, so order generously: try the tuna tartare on miso brioche, the yellowfin tuna “chorizo” (its smoky, paprika-laced punch is balanced by pickled tsukemono and warm pita), or the charred, melt-in-the-mouth octopus with miso, fava beans, and asakura sansho—it’s all rather decadent, but somehow never overly heavy. Come for the pristine, perfectly seasoned nigiri; stay for the golden-hour sunset over the Neoclassical rooftops of this stately corner of central London. —L.H.

Industry observers note that many of the best Japanese restaurants fall into two categories: no-frills neighborhood ramen and udon spots, or the kind of hushed, six-seater omakase counters where you might be frowned at for asking for extra soy sauce. Aki London, tucked inside a soaring, Grade II-listed former bank on Cavendish Square, couldn’t be more different. Designed by Francis Sultana, the dining room is all about pure, flamboyant glamour—think fluted marble columns, soaring coffered ceilings, and plush velvet banquette seating. This isn’t a case of style over substance, however: The kitchen leans into farm-to-table Japanese cooking rooted in Kyoto traditions, ranging from crisp, featherlight tempura rock shrimp to delicate steamed-and-crisped wagyu gyoza, to smoky, tare-brushed chicken thigh skewers straight off the robata grill. Whether you’re coming for a leisurely lunch or a late-night dinner, make sure to check out the subterranean cocktail bar first for a round of yuzu-infused martinis. (Aki is best enjoyed in the tech giant of a lively group.) —L.H.

A neighborhood restaurant in the truest sense, Jin Kichi’s cult following makes booking a table a competitive sport. This tiny, two-floor restaurant is cozy, often crowded, and wonderfully authentic. While the yakitori is a major draw, the sushi and sashimi are of a quality that rivals the city’s most expensive counters. It’s the kind of place where the chefs know the regulars by name (and where stated regulars might be the likes of Kate Moss and Harry Styles). —L.H.

#226659. 37 Thanksgiving Cocktails and Drinks for Every Guest

📅 15 Aug 2016 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1512 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

37 Thanksgiving Cocktails and Drinks for Every Guest

📅 15 Aug 2016 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re pouring a cup of cheer or drinking to steel your nerves against Great-Aunt Edna, these Thanksgiving cocktails cover every angle.
  • And since Thanksgiving is something of a marathon, we’ve included lighter aperitifs and nonalcoholic drinks for anyone looking to pace themselves—or skip the booze altogether.
  • Save recipes and plan every week with confidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re pouring a cup of cheer or drinking to steel your nerves against Great-Aunt Edna, these Thanksgiving cocktails cover every angle. There are the cranberry, apple, and maple flavors we crave this time of year, plus big-batch drinks that won’t keep you playing bartender all afternoon. We’re talking freezer-ready martinis, bourbon punch, and a cranberry mule that guests can spike themselves. After all, your to-do list is long enough.

And since Thanksgiving is something of a marathon, we’ve included lighter aperitifs and nonalcoholic drinks for anyone looking to pace themselves—or skip the booze altogether. When dinner gives way to dessert, warm up with a hot buttered rum, mulled wine, or spiced apple cider. Just don’t forget to set out a few Thanksgiving appetizers while you’re at it.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app.

We love a Paper Plane as much as the next discerning cocktail drinker, but shaking them up one at a time? Hard pass. Batch the bourbon, Aperol, and amaro for this Thanksgiving cocktail ahead, then stir in the lemon juice and water about an hour before serving.

The “upside-down” refers to the inverted ratio of gin and vermouth in these martinis (not what they’ll do to you). The result is a lighter-drinking cocktail you can batch ahead and stash in the freezer until guests arrive.

All the steeped, spiced flavors you love in a hot toddy, with none of the warmth. This icy twist keeps pre-dinner cocktail hour refreshingly chill. Relatives, take note.

Industry observers note that apple cider, tart cranberry juice, and spicy ginger ale give rum punch a seasonal makeover. Make the cranberry-studded ice cubes ahead of time; they’ll keep the punch cold and make each glass look party-ready.

Sure, a cold beer works fine while you're watching football or tending the turkey fryer. But a pitcher of crisp Mexican lager punched up with margarita citrus makes the occasion feel a little more festive. For another low-effort beer cocktail, try a Spaghett—just lager, Aperol, and lemon.

Recent findings suggest that for a massive-batch cocktail with a distinctly autumnal spin, combine rum with dry hard cider and fruit. Prepare the rum base ahead, but save the bubbly cider until just before serving to preserve its fizz.

It has been revealed that bourbon, cognac, floral Earl Grey tea, and an herb-honey syrup make a party-ready punch. For an eye-catching presentation, add an ice ring decorated with lemon slices and rosemary sprigs.

According to recent reports, mezcal, orange liqueur, honey, and chocolate bitters make a lightly smoky cocktail that's particularly good with dessert. Even better, you can batch eight servings and stash them in the freezer up to two weeks ahead. No last-minute shaking required.

According to recent reports, feeling a little gung-ho about Christmas’s fast approach, are we? A major-batch punch packed with cranberry, citrus, nutty sherry, and warming spices makes a delicious bridge between Thanksgiving and the winter holidays.

Sources indicate that A seasonal riff on the French 75 swaps gin for bourbon and adds a homemade pear syrup spiced with cinnamon, ginger, and cloves. We like it for a sparkling toast before dinner or alongside pie afterward.

Industry observers note that the season of Hallmark’s flannel-clad himbos calls for a drink to match. Enter this lower-ABV sipper made with apple cider and amaro. A little bitter, a little sweet, and just fizzy enough—rather like the male lead in whatever movie “your aunt” is watching.

Homemade cranberry-thyme syrup gives this sparkling cocktail its ruby-red glow. A little Campari adds a pleasantly bitter edge, while Champagne makes it worthy of a holiday toast. The syrup can be prepared up to two weeks ahead.

If you want to start Thanksgiving with a little bubbly, this three-ingredient, lower-ABV aperitif is a fine place to begin. The recipe serves four, and the ginger syrup can be made well in advance.

According to recent reports, replace the gin in a classic Negroni with sparkling wine and you’ve got a lighter, fizzy aperitif. The bubbles mellow Campari’s bitter edge, making this a friendly introduction for the Negroni-curious.

Two ingredients, one very good drink. Fino sherry and ginger ale make a lightly boozy, pleasantly dry cocktail with just enough ginger bite.

Industry observers note that botanical gin, bittersweet grapefruit, and sparkling sake make a bubbly cocktail that’s bright enough to cut through a rich Thanksgiving spread. It serves six, so you can pour a round without mixing drinks one by one.

We love a margarita riff no matter the season. Ginger and rosemary bring a distinctly autumnal edge to this fizzy version, with just enough sparkle to make it feel like a holiday toast.

No punch bowls, cocktail shakers, or complicated mixology required for this two-ingredient drink. You’ve got better things to do between hosting duties and getting all those Thanksgiving sides to the table.

Sources indicate that A lower-ABV sipper is your friend during a long day of polite frivolities. The Adonis sounds hella sexy, and we love the earthy nuttiness of sherry and sweet vermouth, made spritzy with club soda.

On a holiday where cranberries overflow-eth, pour a drink to match. Tart, citrusy, and just sweet enough, this vodka cocktail gets its signature pink hue from cranberry juice. A bright counterpoint to all that rich Thanksgiving food.

Sources indicate that A classic old-fashioned needs just bourbon or rye, sugar, and bitters. Making drinks for a crowd? Follow our significant-batch old-fashioned method to prep ahead and avoid playing bartender all Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that think of this as an apple-brandy riff on the Manhattan. Sweet vermouth rounds out the fruit’s warmth, making this a particularly fitting fall cocktail.

Recent findings suggest that not quite a whiskey sour, not quite a cider cocktail, this autumnal drink mixes apple brandy with lemon and orange juices, maple syrup, and a dusting of nutmeg. It tastes like fall without leaning too heavily on baking spices.

Industry observers note that impress your whiskey-loving dad with a Prohibition-era cocktail he may not have heard of. Juicy grapefruit and floral honey give bourbon a bright, citrusy lift, just as winter citrus season is getting underway.

Industry observers note that bourbon, lemon juice, and simple syrup make a tart, boozy drink that’s just sweet enough. It’s ideal for anyone with a minimally stocked bar and a preference for the classics.

Think of the Boulevardier as the Negroni’s bourbon-loving cousin. Whiskey takes the place of gin, bringing warmth and richness to the bittersweet combination of Campari and sweet vermouth. A fine choice for sipping before dinner.

A smoky mezcal cocktail with Earl Grey tea syrup and grapefruit liqueur, this bright, aromatic margarita riff is an intriguing choice for Thanksgiving brunch—or for guests who prefer tequila to bourbon at cocktail hour.

A homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail a distinctly Thanksgiving twist. Lime juice keeps it tart, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim adds a fragrant finish. Make the jam ahead to streamline cocktail hour.

Whether for your Thanksgiving pregame or tomorrow morning’s hair of the dog, a well-made Bloody Mary is always welcome. Worcestershire, horseradish, hot sauce, and fresh lemon give this savory classic its signature kick.

Recent findings suggest that A packed to-do list is no match for this make-ahead drink. Simmer red wine, cider, fruit, and spices ahead of time, then add tawny port and gently reheat when your guests arrive. Keep it warm in a slow cooker for self-service away from the kitchen.

We’d welcome a pot of mulled apple cider at any fall gathering. It’s nonalcoholic, serves a crowd, and fills the kitchen with the scent of warming spices. Guests can add a tipple of brandy, bourbon, Calvados, or rum if they wish.

Can’t decide between hot cider and spice-rich chai? Have both. This cozy, nonalcoholic drink brings tea and warming spices to apple cider, making it a particularly good companion for a second slice of pie.

Sources indicate that for those who’d rather drink their Thanksgiving dessert, a warm mug of dark rum, butter, sugar, and spices delivers the goods. It’s rich, fragrant, and an excellent reason to linger at the table after the pie plates are cleared.

Sources indicate that blood orange, ginger, cinnamon, and cloves make this sweet-tart, nonalcoholic drink feel right at home on Thanksgiving. Prepare the shrub ahead, then top with sparkling water when guests arrive.

Who claims a nonalcoholic spritz can’t have a little attitude? A bittersweet alcohol-free aperitif and a splash of olive brine give this savory, citrusy drink plenty of complexity. Serve it very cold, with an olive garnish.

Industry observers note that green tea, lemon juice, fresh mint, and honey make a soothing tonic after the Thanksgiving bacchanal. Alcohol-free on its own, it can take a splash of mezcal if anyone wants to steer it into cocktail territory.

According to recent reports, spiced maple syrup and cranberry juice reimagine the typical Moscow mule as a Thanksgiving drink that skips the vodka. Note that Angostura bitters contain alcohol; for a completely alcohol-free version, use an alternative like All the Bitter.

Chances are you are reading this while awash in the joyful glow of an active oven and/or open laptop chock full of Black Friday sales. As someone who can’t help but enjoy America’s annual week of consumption, I have some advice: You can probably skip that fourth slice of pie and also, when it comes to gift-giving, bigger is not always better. Personally, some of the best presents I’ve received over the years are small but meaningful items that come with a sense of personal connection and discovery: A set of irresistible Japanese incense from an aspirational boutique my fiancé found in Tokyo’s Aoyama district. Some adorable silk painted ornaments that my mom stumbled upon at a local maker’s market. Employee merch from NASA, where my stepfather worked. All that to say, the ritual of gift-giving is always made to be much more meaningful when we can collect all the little, delightful items we’ve collected over the year and share them with those whom will appreciate them most. Maybe that’s a simple, but utterly practical thingamajig that has made your life that much more convenient. Or something you came across in your travels. Even an item you have at home for years that you couldn’t imagine living without. Here are a few self-care accessories that I've encountered both recently and not-so-recently that fit that bill.

Industry observers note that ever since the days of chewable Flintstones vitamins, we as a human race have been striving for fresh, inventive ways to get our daily dose in. Straight pills are boring and require water. Powders are messy and not easily transported. Gummies can be overly sugary and harden over time. But strips are nearly weightless, easy to travel with, and consumable on their own. The ones made by StripIt dissolve on your tongue, a little like a Listerine mint strip, and come in four different formulas: Vitamin C, D3 + K2, B12, Sleep, and Digest. Though they can take a little bit longer than a mint strip to dissolve, they’re still a really convenient way to make sure you’re keeping up with your supplements. I’ve been using the D3 + K2 ones while I travel. They taste pretty good and are colorful and novel enough to function as a small stocking stuffer or Hanukkah gift for the health hawk in your life.

I will never tire of a big, beautiful block of soap. Especially if it's so fragrant that it fills a whole room with its smell. My new favorite in this category is Life Research Lab, an herb-forward brand that takes inspiration from (and incorporates) the local LA flora into its soap blends. There’s the eucalyptus and grapefruit pumice slab that draws from common neighborhood trees, a classic “cowboy cologne” mix of cypress and California sagebrush so commonly found in Angelenos’ gardens, and a juniper bergamot number that lifts scents from the desert. Many of them contain bits and pieces of the very plants they’re named for, which function as light exfoliants as you scrub. I was especially charmed by the Christmas Morning Soap, which is infused with balsam fir essential oil and pinyon pine leaf. Its name, price, and the fact that it comes in both 9-ounce blocks and 4-ounce cylinders make it a perfect stocking stuffer. T’is the season.

Industry observers note that when I traveled to Seoul a few years ago, I popped into the Hinok store and spent about 20 minutes smelling basically every one of its products, which all contain ingredients sourced by foraging detritus from old cypress forests on Jeju island (not cutting them down). Alas, I couldn’t bring anything home because my carry-on was already stuffed. But recently I learned the brand is available to buy in the US and had a chance to try a few things out. My favorite is the thick, gooey body wash. It has the consistency of honey, and emanates a light, fresh natural scent without being too overpowering. Most crucially, the formula is gentle enough to clean your body without stripping it of its natural oils. After searching for a light body wash I can use daily for a while now, this qucikly became my new favorite. (The deodorising spray is really good for households with pets too.).

When I was in Fresh York last month, my future sister in-law suggested we take a quick field trip to Senti Senti, a little skincare store in Chinatown. To my delight, they carried imported Korean and Japanese formulas of lotions, cleansers, and—most importantly—sunscreen from popular brands like Beauty of Joseon and Bioré. (Don’t ask me how this is allowed, Chinatown’s gonna Chinatown.) In the 15 minutes we spent there, we observed at least three people walk in and beeline for this Dr. Althea face lotion and I couldn’t help but be tempted. Using it for the past month, I’ve been impressed with how light, hydrating, and easily absorbing it is—an excellent goop to apply in the morning. For anyone who hates the lingering feeling of a heavy day cream, this one’s a no-brainer.

We’re days away from the start of winter, meaning we’ll all be heating up our homes and braving, windy, sub-zero temperatures more regularly for the next few months. All of that means our skin has a far higher chance of getting dry and flaky. Enter Bein All-Over Body Oil. The blend of organic sesame seed, squalane, and camellia oil rubs on smoothly and absorbs like a dream, leaving no sticky residue behind. Body oil can be especially helpful for feet, knees, elbows, and hands, post-shower. And is light enough that you can apply lotion on afterward, too. Best of all, the San Diego-brand’s products smell faintly of bitter citrus, like a little Aperol spritz for your skin. It’s bright-red packaging makes it feel especially festive for the holidays.

A good robe, in my humble opinion, must rise to a few crucial tasks. It should be able to absorb water well, dry out rapidly, and let your skin breathe after a long warm soak in the bath or shower. It should also allow you to lounge around your household without flashing your living companions or getting furniture wet. That’s why I’m partial to a long linen kimono, which checks all of those boxes. I was gifted a sophisticated blue-striped one from Deiji Studios nearly six years ago for Christmas, and it’s now a perfectly worn-in, indispensable bathroom staple. No wonder Deiji still sells it. Even better, it’s on sale for Black Friday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

Industry observers note that I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

Recent findings suggest that “We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown confirmed his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” remarked a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

According to recent reports, republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

It has been revealed that but they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

Extra-Fluffy Cinnamon Rolls

💡 Key Takeaways

  • One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, at first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

Sources indicate that the other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

Sources indicate that yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

In a recent development, this is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

According to recent reports, yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

This recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Watch Zaynab perfect these cinnamon rolls.

Whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool.

In a recent development, add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again.

Add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

It has been revealed that while the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

In a recent development, butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes.

Meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable.

Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.

  • All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years.
  • Our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece. Well, as a longtime fragrance editor, I get a similar feeling when I smell Guerlain’s iconic Vétiver scent (or, more recently, Penhaligon’s Halfeti). These fragrances smelled exceptional when they debuted, still do today, probably still will a hundred years from now. And while fragrance, like any art form, has its trends, the truly great scents (and songs) have a way of deflecting them and singing on.

All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years. To do so, I dug through the history of men’s fragrance to put together a list of some of the most iconic colognes of all time. Scents that defined an era, changed the course of perfumery, or smelled so good that folks never stopped wearing them.

Our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time. You might love some more than others, but all have earned their place in the fragrance pantheon. Here are 20 of the most popular, influential, and enduring colognes ever made, and exactly why they’ve lasted.

Industry observers note that is there a more classic cologne than Acqua di Parma’s Colonia? Released in 1916, this timeless citrus is the original Italian splash, and it would be criminal not to include it on a list of this caliber. That crisp, bright citrus opening is unmistakable, but there’s so much more going on beneath the surface as it dries down, with the supporting notes weaving in and out without ever stealing the show. Herbaceous hints of lavender and rosemary add herbal hues, while earthy vetiver and patchouli mingle with the smooth warmth of sandalwood as it settles on the skin. This is one of the great daily drivers, if not the very archetype of what an everyday cologne could or should be. It’s a 10/10 blend of citrus, aromatics, and woods, and more than a century on, still smells as sophisticated as ever.

I’ve written about Guerlain Vétiver so many times, you’d think I’d have run out of ways to sing its praises. But I could go forever. Few fragrances have done more to establish vetiver as a leading note, and since its 1959 debut, this masterpiece has remained every bit as relevant and wearable. It beautifully captures vetiver’s fresher, greener side, rather than leaning into its smoky, earthy character. There’s a crispness, with bright citrus, a touch of spice, and grassy vetiver balanced by subtle tobacco and woods, like the first cool, earthy dew on a spring morning. Elegant and confident, it oozes the kind of sophistication I imagine old-school Hollywood leading men appreciating, yet it wears just as well today, whether you're suited up or simply going about your day.

Ask me to name the most influential luxury fragrance of the 21st century, and there’s a good chance I’d say Aventus (notice, I remarked “luxury”). I’ve seen firsthand just how many guys made their first foray into high-end fragrance with this icon, and while I now often gravitate toward some of the deeper cuts in Creed’s storied catalog, every time I wear Aventus, the compliments roll in. Since its 2010 debut, it has inspired countless imitators and the inevitable fragrance fatigue that comes with being a phenomenon, yet I don’t think it’s lost an ounce of its appeal. To me, it's the ultimate wedding fragrance, a perfect blend of bright citrus and pineapple, aromatic freshness, and rich, smoky woods that’s refined without being fussy. The defining fragrance of the 2010s? I’d make that argument any day. Aventus will always have a place on my shelf.

Recent findings suggest that no. 89 is one of the great British gentlemen’s fragrances, and few colognes capture Bond-like elegance quite like it. And it tracks: Introduced in 1951, No. 89 counted James Bond creator Ian Fleming among its famous admirers, while Cary Grant and Sir Alec Guinness were reportedly devotees as well. The scent itself is traditional in the best way, a classically composed fougère with crisp, almost barbershop-like citrus and lavender freshness, subtle florals, warming spice, and a smooth, woody base of vetiver and oakmoss. Aromatic, gently spicy, and impeccably polished, it’s the olfactory equivalent of a beautifully tailored Savile Row suit. More than seven decades on, No. 89 is proof that class and character never go out of style.

Back in the ’90s, CK One was everywhere. From Wall Street execs to flannel-wearing creatives; its intoxicating freshness just captured the zeitgeist. It was also one of the first mainstream fragrances marketed as unisex. (Almost an afterthought for fragrance fans today, it was a fairly novel concept then.) And while countless fragrances have followed in its footsteps, this citrusy, green, woodsy, lightly sweet profile still more than holds up. A surprising amount is going on here, too: a bright medley of citrus and tropical fruits, a floral heart with hints of spice, and a clean, musky base of cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s an icon that helped define a generation, and it works just as well day or night, on pretty much anyone. And perhaps most impressively, after all these years, CK One still smells unmistakably like CK One.

It has been revealed that much like his clothing, Ralph Lauren’s original Polo fragrance has left an indelible mark on American style. Released in 1978, the unmistakable green-bottled cologne helped define what a classic masculine fragrance could smell like: sophisticated, confident, and unapologetically aromatic. And while nearly five decades have passed, there’s still nothing quite like it. That signature pine-heavy character is front and center, surrounded by a rich blend of herb and spices with bergamot adding brightness and leather lending rugged, earthy depth. It’s bold, woody, green, and distinctly old-school, but that’s precisely its charm. It’s undergone reformulations over the years, and its assertive character won’t appeal to everyone, but there’s no denying its place in the fragrance hall of fame. Some colognes come and go, but Polo isn’t going anywhere.

When I spotted that frosted bottle in my dad’s medicine cabinet and wore it for the first time, I had no idea that this scent would spark a lifelong fragrance obsession. Armani’s 1996 icon, Acqua di Giò, has been worn by millions, referenced endlessly, and spawned countless flankers, but the original remains one of those rare mass-appeal designer colognes that have stood the test of time. Why? Because it’s just so wearable. Long before the niche fragrance boom, when designer colognes dominated department store counters, Acqua di Giò caught on like wildfire, appealing to just about every kind of guy, whether for the office or date night. At its core is a beautifully nuanced blend of citrus, fresh marine accords, and soft florals, grounded by a musky amber base. On skin, it’s breezy, clean, and subtly woody, with an oceanic quality. If you’ve never rocked it or haven’t reached for it in years, do yourself a favor and revisit this classic.

Imitation is the highest form of flattery, and so many colognes still try to smell like Cool Water. Introduced in 1988, it became a full-blown phenomenon in the ’90s, and for a generation of guys, it was practically a rite of passage. Along with CK One, it was non-negotiable during my formative years, and even then, before I’d developed my own distinct taste, I knew I didn’t want to smell like everyone else. But there was something about this intoxicating green aquatic I just couldn’t resist. Its blend of lavender, mint, rosemary, and neroli nodded to classic gentleman’s fougères, but Cool Water took that aromatic DNA somewhere fresh—a singular scent that’s herbal and richly marine, softened by a woody, musky warmth. While it might smell dated to some, there’s no denying its place among the most iconic fragrances of all time, and I’d argue it still smells amazing on the right dude, especially on a spring or summer day.

Terre d’Hermès is (probably) my favorite designer fragrance of all time. When Jean-Claude Ellena created it back in 2006, he delivered something entirely different from the crowd-pleasing designer colognes of the day. There’s an earthiness to it that I find irresistible, a marriage of citrus, dry woods, spice, and that unmistakable flinty, mineral character that gives it so much personality. It’s sophisticated without being stuffy, with a gorgeous, almost boozy warmth that makes it feel sultry and downright sexy. I particularly love wearing it in colder weather, when those warm, woody facets really come alive, but I can reach for it almost anytime. Plenty of designer colognes are simply pleasant, but Terre d’Hermès is distinctive and endlessly wearable.

Few colognes in modern history have generated as much conversation, inspired as many memes, or become quite as zeitgeist-y as Dior Sauvage. Love it or roll your eyes at its popularity, its influence on modern men’s perfumery is undeniable. Since its debut in 2015, Sauvage has become one of the world’s bestselling fragrances, at times even claiming the number-one spot. And it’s easy to see why. That unmistakable blend of citrus, spice, and all things ambery nice is crisp and fresh, with a warm, woody drydown that’s oh so smooth. It’s a crowd-pleaser in the truest sense, versatile enough to wear just about anywhere, though I think it really shines after dark. Sauvage has since spawned an entire family of flankers, but the original EDT started it all.

In a recent development, you've smelled Bleu de Chanel on plenty of guys. A beautifully composed citrus-spice-wood classic, it works just as well with a navy suit as it does with a white tee and jeans. Note: When Chanel's legendary perfumer Jacques Polge introduced it in 2010, he didn't just create another handsome, crowd-pleasing cologne; he helped define the modern blue fragrance, a fresh, clean, citrusy, and woody genre that's become a mainstay. Sixteen years on, the original remains one of the most approachable and endlessly versatile colognes ever. Its bright citrus opening gives way to an aromatic blend of cool mint, warming spices, and subtle florals, all grounded by a rich, woody base with touches of earthy vetiver, patchouli, and resinous warmth. There really is only one Bleu.

Recent findings suggest that this was a tough call. Ask any scent head about Tom Ford's fragrances, and they’ll surely bring up Neroli Portofino and Tobacco Vanille, both arguably just as iconic (and good) as this one. But if you polled fans on the most influential Tom Ford fragrances, I think Oud Wood would edge out the competition. Launched in 2007, it helped introduce Oud to a broader Western audience, making the traditionally intense ingredient feel approachable. It’s elegant and beautifully blended, with a smoky, almost creamy heart of oud, sandalwood, and rosewood, accented by subtle spice and the warmth of vanilla and amber. It’s heady yet easy to wear, with an addictive richness that never wears thin.

Sources indicate that I’ve worn pretty much every Le Labo under the sun, and while my personal favorites lean toward the eucalyptus and vetiver side of the house, there’s simply no telling the story of modern perfumery without Santal 33. Love it or find it utterly overplayed, you’ve smelled it. Since its 2011 debut, it’s wafted through elevators, the backseats of cabs, countless weddings and date nights, and just about everywhere in between. More importantly, it helped bring sandalwood into the mainstream, and became a reference point for an entire genre of warm, woody fragrances. But before everyone started rocking it, Santal 33 was, and still is, a brilliant composition: creamy sandalwood, dry cedar, cardamom spice, and leathery warmth. It’s a niche legend that has suffered from its own success, yes, but give it another ten years, and don’t be surprised if the very fragrance many got tired of smelling becomes cool all over again.

If you’re remotely a scent head, chances are you dig at least one, if not several, of Parfums de Marly’s fragrances (my personal favorite is the oud-praline magic that is Haltane). But if I had to sum up the house in one word, it would be regal. It does refined, layered elegance exceptionally well, and while some folks might champion Althaïr or Castley, to my nose, the fougère-forward Layton best epitomizes the house. Released in 2016, it’s one of the finest fougères I’ve ever smelled, rich yet airy, with classic lavender reimagined alongside crisp apple, bright citrus, cardamom, woods, and a healthy dose of vanilla. It’s practically the template for what a modern fougère aspires to be, and its enduring popularity suggests plenty of fragrance fans would agree. It doesn’t hurt that the matte blue bottle with its signature silver dome is so flauntworthy.

Recent findings suggest that few fragrances in recent times have had the same cultural impact as Baccarat Rouge 540, becoming a signature scent for everyone from socialites to fragrance obsessives. Yes, it's polarizing, and some might argue its ubiquity has stripped it of some of its magic. But it's become a modern classic for a reason, starting with the masterful nose behind it: Francis Kurkdjian, founder of his namesake maison. Introduced in 2015, it's a luminous floral amber, with saffron lending spice, jasmine bringing a soft warmth, and a generous dose of amberwood creating that glowing aura. Sultry, heady, and diffusive, it's a straight-up unisex phenomenon that smells a little different on everyone who wears it, yet still unveils itself before you even enter a room. Whether you're a devotee or a detractor, there's no denying it's left its mark.

It came down to Bal d’Afrique and Gypsy Water, though plenty of Byredo fragrances could have earned a spot here. But I’m the editor, and I’m going with my all-time favorite from one of the houses that helped bring niche perfumery into the mainstream. Launched in 2008, Gypsy Water was one of the first niche fragrances I ever fell for, and it holds such a special place in my heart that I still wear it regularly. There’s something almost holy about its airy blend of incense, soft woods, bright lemon, and a whisper of vanilla and amber, all coming together with that subtle yet magnetic, almost skin-scent quality Byredo does so well. Artsy, chic, and easy to love, this woody aromatic never tries too hard to make an impression yet often leaves a lasting one.

It has been revealed that since its 2015 debut, Xerjoff’s Naxos has achieved near-mythic status, winning over everyone from fragrance-obsessed TikTokers to yacht-owning gentlemen with decidedly expensive taste. And I get it. This is an almost impossibly well-blended composition that somehow manages to be both decadent and incredibly wearable, making it a great place to start if you’re looking to venture into niche perfumery. On paper, the combination of tobacco, aromatic lavender, fruity freshness, and a prominent honey accord sounds like it shouldn’t quite work, but man, does it ever. That rich sweetness is a defining feature, especially in the opening, before the herbal, earthy tones and a hefty dose of vanilla come together in a downright sumptuous yet crisp way. The hype may have quieted down since its social media heyday, but Naxos deserves its flowers as a modern niche standout.

Halfeti has become a signature of mine, though I’m admittedly a little late to the game, having received my first bottle as a birthday gift last year, well after it had achieved iconic status in scent circles. But better late than never, especially when a fragrance is this good. Named after a Turkish town known for its roses, it leans into a rich, heady floral style, layered with citrus, herbs, and spice. Bergamot and grapefruit lift the opening before saffron and cardamom give way to a deep base of leather, oud, cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s a lot, but it all hangs together gorgeously, creating a woody, spicy, aromatic scent that’s elegant and sexy, perfect for special occasions or date nights. But I’d happily wear it just about anywhere, including when I’m not going anywhere at all.

Musc Ravageur embodies the risk-taking spirit of niche perfumery. Launched in 2000, it helped redefine what a modern musk fragrance could be at a time when fresh, clean fragrances dominated the men’s market. More than a quarter century later, it remains a cult favorite, thanks in no small part to its warm, almost funky (in a good way) richness. It opens with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and rose, all resting on a base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. A benchmark for animalic musks, it’s an alluring, sultry, and unapologetically sensual aroma, equally suited to being a signature scent or an olfactory companion for wherever the evening leads.

Recent findings suggest that amouage has dropped so many olfactory bangers over the years that choosing just one for this list wasn't easy. The Omani house has built its reputation on rich, complex compositions that keep you coming back to sniff your pulse points, and while I could make a case for several of its fragrances, Reflection Man feels quintessentially Amouage. Released in 2007, it’s become a luxury niche benchmark, proving that a floral-forward fragrance can be every bit as rich and sophisticated as its woody or spicy counterparts. It opens with an herbaceous blend of rosemary, berries, and orange before orris, jasmine, and ylang-ylang bring a lush, earthy depth, all grounded by a smooth base of vetiver, patchouli, and sandalwood. The result is a layered floral-woody scent that’s distinctive without being difficult to wear, and versatile enough for everything from a boardroom to a black-tie gala. Pricey, yes, but worth every spritz.

In a recent development, black Friday 2026 is officially here, and although I’ve been keeping tabs on all the Black Friday clothing deals for weeks, there’s something to be mentioned about playing the waiting game. Whatever you’re shopping for this time around—whether it’s winter wardrobe upgrades, a refresh of closet essentials, a little holiday outfitting, or some particularly good gifts—consider this your edit of the best Black Friday clothing deals worth knowing about.

Industry observers note that I always make a point to peruse the offerings at major retailers like Net-a-Porter, Nordstrom, and Shopbop, where some of the most coveted designer pieces are finally marked down. But this year, I’ve been particularly taken with the under-the-radar private sales, too. We’ve sifted through hundreds (really!) to uncover the ones worth your attention, from Aflalo and Kallmeyer to Connor Ives and beyond—the kind of discoveries that delight even the most seasoned Vogue editors.

Shop all our favorites in this running master list of Black Friday clothing sales, and be sure to check back throughout the weekend as we continue tracking the best deals leading into Cyber Monday.

For more sale edits, check out our guide to the best Black Friday jewelry deals and the Black Friday beauty deals, with closer looks at the offerings at Zara, Banana Republic, Leset.

It has been revealed that net-a-Porter’s sale section is filled with more than 12,000 pieces marked up to 50% off across nearly every apparel and accessories category imaginable. Think luxe outerwear, cozy knits, shoes, and handbags—all ideal for elevating your fall wardrobe. Among my favorite finds: Tove’s shearling-trimmed leather coat and Khaite’s leopard-print knee-high boots—two statement-makers this New Yorker can certainly get behind.

If your denim drawer is needing a seasonal upgrade, Levi’s is offering 40% off the site for Black Friday, which includes free shipping and returns—score! The promotion includes forever-classic fits like the 501, as well as slouchier styles like the Low Loose. Beyond denim, I’m stocking up on a few of my favorite white T-shirts and have my eye on to round out my essentials drawer.

There are plenty of gems to uncover in Nordstrom’s Black Friday sale offerings, from high fashion to winter fitness apparel (think leggings and joggers). My top picks for Cyber Week include Burberry’s classic khaki trench coat and Toteme’s iconic T-Lock bag in cognac—two timeless pieces I know I’d wear on repeat.

It has been revealed that the Shopbop sale is a go-to for contemporary fashion finds that feel both on-trend and wallet-friendly, and they’ve made the art of shopping Black Friday deals extremely easy. Use code HOLIDAY to receive 25% off the site, including the sale section. Marc Jacobs’s leopard-print winter jacket is already in my cart, while a new pair of A.Emery’s black loafers is a no-brainer addition.

Gap’s sale for Black Friday is on and they’re offering 50% off the entire site, with even more savings on their favorite gift ideas. Stock up on everyday essentials (sweatpants and sweatshirts not pictured!) and your future self will thank you. A bold red knit and brown corduroy pants are at the top of my cart.

Uniqlo’s reliable lineup of everyday essentials is even more tempting with limited-time deals in their limited-time Black Friday deals. I’ve already grabbed this flannel shirt and a few of their Heattech turtlenecks to layer underneath my puffer coat—and I’m going back for multiple colors, because the cold snap is no joke. These make navigating the Northeast’s ever-changing temperatures a little easier.

Don’t sleep on J.Crew’s Black Friday deals. Think 40% off the entire site, 50% off almost all pajamas, and an extra 40% off all sale pieces. It’s the perfect excuse to scoop up those timeless wardrobe staples, cozy sleepwear, and a few special finds you’ve been eyeing. This suede bomber jacket is finally going to be mine—and my black trouser collection could certainly use another addition (or two).

Industry observers note that black Friday arrives and Banana Republic’s sale is a safe bet for everyday winter clothing with a twist. How cute is this plaid dress for cozy holiday gatherings? I’ve also been in the market for a new leather work tote to carry my laptop, and this feels like the perfect opportunity to invest in one that’s both polished and practical—especially at this price point.

The deals are rolling in, and Vogue editors like myself are heading straight to Leset, where the entire site is 25% off. Refreshing your essentials drawer is a breeze, whether you’re stocking up on the T-shirts Jennifer Lawrence loves. I’m also eyeing this chic car coat—a timeless outerwear buy that Kendall Jenner has been spotted in.

Sources indicate that some of the season’s most coveted pieces are now up to 50% off in Bloomingdale’s end-of-season deals, where the more you buy, the more you save. My instant standouts include Toteme’s scarf-neck jacket and Róhe’s lace-trimmed camisole, both of which I can already envision styling in countless ways. Plus, regular-price items are 25% off for Black Friday only.

One really good private sale worth getting excited about? The Row. I gave up on their IRL sample sales a few years ago, after waiting in line for hours without entry. Now, I don’t have to. From luxe knitwear to buttery leather bags, these investment-worthy pieces rarely come around at prices like these—and who knows how long they will last.

Recent findings suggest that the private sales are quickly becoming the best-kept secret for major deals this season—and I did a double take when Khaite’s email hit my inbox. The iconic Samuel leather jacket? 40% off. The Jett D’Orsay pumps? 50% off! And that’s just the tip of the iceberg. Safe to say, my wish list continues to grow.

Fashion girls know that Nour Hammour is the go-to for statement outerwear—just ask Dakota Johnson, who’s been spotted several times this fall in the Parisian label’s covetable coats. From shearling-trimmed coats to suede skirts, the brand is making a case for my winter wardrobe refresh—especially with savings up to 50% off.

The designer sale has broken at Bergdorf Goodman, with latest markdowns dropping daily! One of my favorite standout finds includes a satin parka from Maria McManus. If you’re in the market for a good bag, there are plenty of investment-worthy styles to add to your cart, too. Did someone say Alaïa?

Industry observers note that ring the alarm! A hand-picked selection of Nike best sellers is 25% off for Black Friday. Simply use code BFRIDAY at checkout to score the savings. From puffers to workout essentials (this sports bra is a personal go-to of mine!) and the V5 RNR sneakers Hailey Bieber is often spotted in, there’s plenty worth adding to your rotation.

Industry observers note that tory Burch’s Holiday Event is on, and shoppers can take 30% off when spending $250 or more. Go ahead, lean into a little seasonal indulgence. From faux-shearling coats to a calf-hair-print version of the Pierced mules, these statement-making finds will bring a little extra personality to any wardrobe.

It has been revealed that for Black Friday, Staud is offering 30% off site-wide, plus an additional 30% off the sale section. That means timeless wardrobe classics, like the Wally boots (in brown suede!), are finally within reach. Or, if your holiday party wardrobe could use a little refresh, there’s nothing a sparkly beaded bag can’t do to brighten even the most understated outfit.

Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I’m tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients.
  • This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs.
  • According to recent reports, you’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I’m tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients. With 26 grams of protein and just 25 minutes of prep-and-cook time, HelloFresh’s Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl is a great solution for dinner.

This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

According to recent reports, you’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

Industry observers note that true to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how rapidly they pinked up.

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

This is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

According to recent reports, would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover newly introduced flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table rapidly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.

What is the best nose hair trimmer?

According to recent reports, the best men’s nose hair trimmer is Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer 5000 Series, according to GQ. The powerful device offers dual trimming options (for internal and peripheral nostril hairs) and also functions as a facial hair, eyebrow, and ear hair trimmer.

Can a nose hair trimmer cut you?

Sources indicate that whether you are using a rotary head or a linear head, nose hair trimmers are built with a protective guard, which ensures the blade doesn’t come in direct contact with the skin. The protective guard also helps you get a clean cut so the device doesn’t pull or pluck at your nose hairs. Generally speaking, nose hair trimmers do not hurt.

Recent findings suggest that not only can nose hair trimmers be washed, but it is notable to disinfect them between use, first by flushing out stray hair clippings. Let them dry before storing, too, to avoid rust and bacterial proliferation between each use. It’s a good idea to clean the device again before using it, since it is going into your nose, after all.

Do you need a nose hair trimmer, and how often should you use it?

If visible nose hairs bother you, a trimmer is a simple way to keep them tidy. There’s no fixed schedule to follow – a quick trim when hairs start showing is usually all that’s needed. Concentrate on those visible hairs around the nostril opening, rather than trying to remove everything inside. Ear hair and eyebrows can be tidied as needed, using the appropriate attachment and comb.

How do you use a nose hair trimmer?

Industry observers note that to trim your nose hair, simply stick the trimming tip of the device in your nostril and apply a gentle circular motion. Here are a few more tips to keep in mind, according to Simone:.

How do I clean my nose hair trimmer?

The cleaning systems for nose hair trimmers vary. “Some nose hair trimmers are waterproof, so it’s easy to just rinse under water, if you are the sole user, and just let it air dry,” says Simone. If you share the device with somebody else, then it’s going to be all the more vital that you disinfect between uses (ideally before and after each trim). “Make sure you have tapped out the hair trapped inside to avoid clogging,” adds Simone. “For a disinfectant, I would use a sterilizing alcohol pad or barber’s disinfectant, and just wipe the tool gently dry.”.

Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts
